# Stock Market Today: Nasdaq Surges Toward Correction Exit as CPI Hits 3.3%, CRWV Jumps 8% on Anthropic Deal — Dow Slides 101 Points

## S&P 500 eyes eighth straight winning session at 6,837 as gasoline prices explode 21.2%, core inflation holds at 0.2%, and TSMC smashes revenue records with 35% growth | That's TradingNEWS

TradingNEWS Archive 4/10/2026 12:00:18 PM

### Key Points

- Nasdaq rises 0.58% to 22,957 while Dow drops 101 points as March CPI hits 3.3% annually, driven by a 21.2% gasoline surge — core inflation holds tame at 0.2%.
- CoreWeave (CRWV) surges 8% after securing a multi-year Anthropic deal. TSMC (TSM) climbs 2.93% to $376 after reporting record Q1 revenue of $35.71B, up 35% year-over-year.
- Consumer sentiment collapses to 47.6 in April as $98 WTI crude and $4-plus gas prices squeeze households. Fed rate cut odds rise to 29.8% after softer-than-expected core CPI.

Friday's session is operating on two completely separate engines, and the gap between them is telling a story that cuts deeper than a simple risk-on, risk-off narrative. The Nasdaq Composite is pushing 0.58% higher to 22,957, threading toward its eighth consecutive winning session and positioned to exit correction territory entirely — a milestone that would represent a full round-trip recovery from the panic selling that gripped technology shares when the Middle East conflict first erupted. The S&P 500 is clinging to a 0.19% gain at 6,837, not a strong print but directionally constructive given the weight of the macro data that landed before the open. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is quietly bleeding, down 101 points or 0.21% to 48,083, dragged by its energy and industrial composition at a moment when those sectors are absorbing the secondary effects of $98 oil. The Russell 2000 is barely breathing at 2,635, off 0.03%, as small-cap names remain caught between improving risk sentiment and genuine concern about domestic demand destruction at the consumer level. The VIX dropped 2.57% to 18.99, and that number matters — it's no longer pricing in acute crisis, which tells you the market has mechanically absorbed the worst of the ceasefire uncertainty and is now operating in a zone of uneasy equilibrium rather than outright fear. None of this is euphoria. It's a market that got less bad news than it feared and is repricing accordingly, one sector at a time.

#### Why the Index Divergence Is the Real Signal Right Now

The split between the Dow and the Nasdaq on a day like this isn't cosmetic. It reflects a fundamental disagreement about where the economy goes from here. Dow components are disproportionately exposed to energy costs, transportation economics, industrial margins, and consumer spending on physical goods — all of which are under direct pressure from six weeks of elevated crude oil prices and a Strait of Hormuz that remains largely closed despite the ceasefire. Nasdaq components, by contrast, are weighted toward software, semiconductors, and AI infrastructure — areas where the demand signal is structural rather than cyclical and where the Iran conflict creates noise but not existential risk to the earnings thesis. When the Nasdaq is up 0.58% and the Dow is down 0.21% on the same CPI print, the market is essentially saying it believes the energy shock is a bounded, temporary event rather than a systemic demand problem — at least for now. The consumer sentiment data released this morning at 47.6 is the main challenge to that interpretation, and the tension between those two readings — a resilient tech rally and a collapsing consumer confidence number — is the central unresolved contradiction in Friday's tape.

#### March CPI Comes In Hot on the Surface, But the Core Tells a Different Story

The headline number was jarring enough to stop anyone cold the moment it crossed. March CPI printed at 0.9% month-over-month and 3.3% year-over-year — the steepest annual climb since May 2024 and a violent acceleration from February's readings of 0.3% monthly and 2.4% annually. On a surface read, that's a stagflation signal. But decomposing the number reveals something far more nuanced and ultimately more important for how rates, equities, and the dollar trade from here. The energy index alone surged 10.9% in a single calendar month. Gasoline specifically exploded 21.2% — the single largest monthly gain in that series since the Bureau of Labor Statistics began tracking it in 1967. That one line item, gasoline, accounted for nearly three-quarters of the entire monthly headline CPI increase. Everything else was either flat or modestly positive. Strip energy and food out of the calculation entirely, and core CPI came in at just 0.2% month-over-month and 2.6% year-over-year, landing materially below the 0.3% consensus estimate that Wall Street had priced in. That core undershoot is the real news of this report, and it's why markets are not selling off the way the headline 3.3% print might suggest they should. Airfares climbed 2.7% in March after a 1.4% move in February, and on an annual basis they are now up 14.9% — a direct transmission mechanism from jet fuel costs to ticket prices that is working exactly as the economic textbook would predict. Food was essentially flat in aggregate, though the granular category data shows genuine volatility beneath the surface. Tomatoes rose 15.3% in a single month, while hot dogs fell 3.6%. Pasta prices moved, produce prices moved, but there was no broad-based food inflation acceleration that would suggest the energy shock is bleeding into agricultural supply chains in a sustained way. Not yet.

#### The Gasoline Shock Is a Supply Story, Not a Demand Story — and That Changes Everything

Jerome Powell has been making this distinction explicitly for weeks, and the CPI data released Friday validates his framing in a way that gives the Fed genuine intellectual cover to stay put. The Strait of Hormuz closure is a textbook supply shock. Roughly 20% of global crude oil and a significant portion of liquefied natural gas transits that chokepoint daily. When Iran effectively closed it six weeks ago, the physical availability of oil to global markets contracted without any change in underlying demand. Prices rose not because American consumers or businesses suddenly wanted more energy, but because the supply pipeline was physically interrupted by a geopolitical event. That distinction matters enormously for monetary policy because a central bank raising rates to fight supply-shock inflation does not solve the supply problem — it simply layers demand destruction on top of a supply constraint, which is the worst possible combination for an economy. The Fed's institutional memory of 2022, when they were late to recognize genuine demand-pull inflation, makes them appropriately cautious about symmetrically over-reacting to what is clearly a different animal. Jeffrey Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, put the forward-looking problem clearly and without softening it: another one or two hot inflation prints should be expected as the full April impact works its way through transportation services and durable goods categories, and the secondary effects will likely add another 0.2 percentage points over the coming months. He explicitly stated the Fed is on hold through the next several meetings. That view is now consensus. Brian Jacobsen at Annex Wealth Management acknowledged the shock was startling in print even when fully anticipated, but noted there are zero signs yet that elevated energy costs are seeping into core inflation in a self-sustaining way. Oxford Economics' lead U.S. economist Bernard Yaros drew the 2022 comparison explicitly and then rejected it — noting that global supply chain stress indicators are not flashing red, which is a critical differentiation from the post-pandemic environment where every supply chain was simultaneously under pressure. The energy shock is severe, localized, and war-dependent. That's a different policy problem than 2022.

#### Fed Rate Cut Odds Shift Meaningfully After the Core Print

The probability distribution around Fed policy shifted in real time after the CPI release. Odds of the FOMC holding rates flat through the full calendar year fell from 71.1% on Thursday to 64.5% Friday morning. Odds of at least one quarter-point cut arriving before year-end climbed from 24.4% to 29.8% — and the comparison to just 11.8% a week ago shows how quickly the rate cut narrative can re-accelerate when core inflation cooperates. What's driving this is straightforward: if core CPI is running at 2.6% year-over-year with a 0.2% monthly print, the underlying inflation dynamics outside of the war-driven energy shock are actually moving in the right direction. The Fed's preferred PCE measure will tell a slightly different story when it reports, but the directional message from core CPI is that non-energy inflation pressure is not building. The 10-year Treasury yield at 4.31% is up 2 basis points on the session — mild selling in bonds — which reflects the residual concern that April and May CPI prints will be worse before they get better. The market is not declaring victory on inflation, but it's no longer bracing for a scenario where the energy shock becomes a core inflation problem. The difference between those two scenarios is the difference between rate cuts later this year and rate hikes — and Friday's data firmly tilted the probability distribution toward the former.

#### Kevin Warsh's Fed Chair Hearing Goes Cold at the Worst Possible Moment

There's a separate layer of institutional uncertainty surrounding the Federal Reserve that has received insufficient attention relative to the economic stakes. Kevin Warsh, Trump's nominee to succeed Jerome Powell as Fed Chair, was scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on April 16. That hearing has been delayed. The committee has not yet received Warsh's financial disclosures, and the panel's own procedural rules require a minimum one-week advance notice before any hearing can be convened. Three separate people familiar with the Senate process confirmed the paperwork has not been submitted. The committee cannot schedule the hearing until the documentation arrives, and even then there's a mandatory waiting period before proceedings begin. In normal times, a delayed confirmation hearing is inside baseball. In the current environment — where the Fed is managing a war-driven energy shock, navigating the most complex inflation environment in years, operating with a rate structure that has barely moved in months, and facing potential pressure from the White House to ease — the question of who chairs that institution matters enormously for market credibility. Powell's term as Chair runs through May 2026. The nomination timeline is becoming genuinely tight, and a prolonged confirmation limbo adds an institutional overhang on monetary policy that the market has not priced with any precision.

#### CRWV Pops Nearly 8% on Multi-Year Anthropic Deal — Nine of Ten AI Model Providers Now on Its Platform

CoreWeave (CRWV) is the most decisive momentum trade on the tape Friday, up 7.9% to $99.27 in morning trading. The company announced a multi-year agreement with Anthropic under which CoreWeave's cloud infrastructure will handle compute workloads for Claude, Anthropic's flagship AI model family. The strategic implication of the deal is substantial. CoreWeave is now claiming that nine out of ten AI model providers run on its platforms — a market penetration figure that, if accurate, positions the company as the de facto backbone of the commercial AI compute stack in a way that no single contract can fully capture. Winning Anthropic specifically matters for a different reason: Anthropic is one of the most capital-intensive and compute-hungry model developers in the space, with training runs and inference workloads that demand not just capacity but reliability at scale. A multi-year deal means committed revenue visibility, not spot pricing, and that distinction carries enormous weight for a company that went public amid skepticism about whether its infrastructure could sustain enterprise-grade commitments at the level its valuation implied. The AI infrastructure buildout has survived every macro disruption thrown at it this year — tariff fears, war-driven energy cost increases, rate uncertainty — and CoreWeave's partnership momentum suggests the demand side of that equation is durable at a level the broader market keeps underestimating. This is a BUY on the pull on any meaningful dip. The revenue visibility from committed multi-year model developer contracts is exactly the kind of structural anchor that separates CoreWeave from speculative compute plays.

#### TSMC Reports Record Q1 Revenue at $35.71 Billion — 35% Growth Silences the Bears

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) is up 2.93% to $376.20 after delivering a Q1 revenue report that directly refuted the most bearish scenario the market had constructed around the Iran conflict. January through March revenue came in at T$1.134 trillion, equivalent to $35.71 billion in U.S. dollar terms. That number beat the LSEG SmartEstimate compiled from 20 analysts of T$1.125 trillion and landed squarely within TSMC's own guidance range of $34.6 billion to $35.8 billion that management provided at the January earnings call. Year-over-year, this represents a 35% revenue expansion — a record quarter by any measure. The bear case coming into this print was straightforward: if the Middle East war is raising energy costs and disrupting global supply chains for production materials, data center operators might delay or scale back AI infrastructure investment, which would flow through to reduced advanced node wafer demand at TSMC and softer revenue guidance. That thesis is now demonstrably wrong for Q1, and the analyst community is rapidly revising Q2 higher. The April-June consensus revenue estimate has already been lifted 2.3% over the past 30 days to a record T$1.2 trillion. The structural bet embedded in that revision is that advanced AI chip production capacity remains constrained enough that TSMC's pricing power stays intact even if macro conditions remain choppy. NVIDIA (NVDA) traded up 1.9% to $187.44 in sympathy — a logical move given that NVDA is TSMC's largest advanced node customer by revenue concentration. Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya raised his global semiconductor 2026 revenue outlook to $1.3 trillion on the back of continued AI-driven demand for compute, networking, and memory. Gartner separately confirmed the $1.3 trillion figure, calling it the industry's third consecutive year of double-digit growth. The four-year projection to $2 trillion implies a 20% compound annual growth rate for an industry that has historically tracked closer to 8-10%. The gap between that implied rate and historical norms is the AI premium — and TSMC's Q1 print suggests the market is right to pay it. TSM is a BUY. The record revenue, the guidance beat, the upward analyst revisions on Q2, and the structural demand from AI data center expansion make this one of the highest-conviction long setups in global equity markets today.

#### Semiconductor Supply Chain Confirmed Intact — Photonics Bookings Extend to 2027

The AI infrastructure buildout confirmation doesn't stop at TSMC. Lumentum Holdings jumped 5% in premarket after its CEO delivered one of the most bullish forward statements in the sector this earnings cycle, telling Bloomberg directly that the company's optical and photonic product lines are completely booked through 2027. That's a two-year-plus order book in a business that typically operates with shorter lead times, and it represents genuine industrial demand confirmation rather than guidance language or management optimism. Coherent, another photonics company with direct Nvidia investment exposure, moved up 4% on the coattails of the same sector narrative. The photonics layer of the AI supply chain sits below the semiconductor layer in the stack — these are the components that move data between chips, between servers, and between data center buildings at the optical transmission speeds that modern AI workloads require. Without scaling photonic interconnect capacity, data centers cannot scale compute regardless of how many GPUs they install. Booking visibility through 2027 in this segment is a structural signal about how far ahead data center operators are planning their buildouts, and it's bullish for the entire AI infrastructure chain from silicon to optical to power to cooling. Both names are BUY-rated in this environment — the forward booking confirmation at Lumentum specifically removes the demand uncertainty that has been the primary overhang on photonics valuations for the past two quarters.

#### Shake Shack Gets a Clear Upgrade With 23% Upside Baked In

Shake Shack (SHAK) is trading up 2.09% to $99.59 following a Mizuho upgrade from neutral to outperform and a price target hike from $100 to $120, implying 23% upside from Thursday's close. The upgrade thesis from analyst Nick Setyan is multi-layered and deserves unpacking. On the top line, Mizuho's channel checks point to Q1 same-store sales growth coming in above current street estimates — a direct revenue upside signal before the quarter has even been reported. The comp drivers include expanded marketing spend, a broadened value menu designed to retain traffic in an environment where the consumer is feeling gasoline price pressure, and the upcoming FIFA World Cup, which Setyan explicitly names as a significant incremental traffic event. On the margin side, Setyan is projecting high-teens annual EBITDA growth in both 2026 and 2027 — comparing that to Shake Shack's own compound annual EBITDA growth rate of 16% from 2019 to 2024 and the peer group average of low-20% growth. The supply chain efficiency component is the margin story: if Shake Shack can maintain or expand restaurant-level margins even as input costs fluctuate, the operating leverage in the model becomes disproportionately powerful at this revenue scale. At $99 with a credible fundamental path to $120 supported by traffic catalysts, operational improvement, and analyst conviction, SHAK is a BUY. The World Cup tailwind alone — increased foot traffic, higher throughput per location, elevated beverage attachment rates — is a meaningful near-term earnings driver that the market hasn't fully incorporated.

#### Palo Alto and CrowdStrike Bounce After Claude Mythos Partnership Skepticism Destroyed Them Thursday

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) and CrowdStrike are each recovering more than 2% Friday after both names took a significant hit Thursday when market confidence in a reported partnership with Anthropic around the Claude Mythos model evaporated. The Thursday selloff was sharp — both stocks dropped hard as traders concluded that the AI integration narrative that had been driving premium valuations in enterprise cybersecurity was either overblown, premature, or not translating into concrete revenue. Friday's bounce is a relief trade, not a conviction reversal. The underlying question of how deeply AI model integration translates into real incremental revenue for pure-play cybersecurity firms remains fundamentally unanswered. Palo Alto has been building its platformization narrative for two years, arguing that consolidating security functions onto a single AI-enhanced platform creates a durable competitive moat and accelerates revenue per customer. CrowdStrike's Falcon platform makes similar structural claims. Both theses have merit as long-term operating stories. But neither company has yet produced the kind of concrete revenue evidence that would justify treating AI as a current-year earnings driver rather than a multiyear optionality story. PANW and CrowdStrike are both HOLD. Until the Claude Mythos integration — or whatever AI partnership eventually takes shape — gets quantified in terms of contract size, customer additions, or revenue impact, the premium embedded in these valuations needs to earn its keep through execution rather than narrative.

#### ServiceNow Takes a Structural Confidence Hit From UBS — Downgrade Isn't About the Business, It's About Certainty

ServiceNow fell 1.5% premarket after UBS shifted its rating from buy to neutral, and the language of the downgrade is worth taking seriously. UBS had previously argued that ServiceNow was relatively better positioned than most enterprise software peers to navigate and benefit from the AI transformation — a thesis built around the company's workflow automation capabilities being natural infrastructure for AI agent deployment. The downgrade doesn't reverse that structural view entirely. What it says is that UBS's confidence in that view has diminished to the point where the buy rating is no longer justified at current price levels. That's a different kind of negative signal from a straight business deterioration call. It's a valuation confidence call — the market needs to see ServiceNow actually delivering on the AI workflow thesis in reported revenue before paying a growth premium for it. At current multiples, uncertainty is expensive. ServiceNow is a HOLD until execution provides the evidence that UBS — and the broader market — needs to rebuild conviction in the AI revenue story.

#### Consumer Sentiment Collapses to 47.6 — The Real Economy Is Sending a Warning

The University of Michigan's preliminary April consumer sentiment index fell to 47.6 from March's reading of 53.3, a decline of approximately 11% in a single month and a level that sits about 9% below where it was a year ago. Context is important here: 47.6 is not just a bad number, it's historically bad. Readings at that level have historically been associated with consumers who expect economic conditions to deteriorate materially — not consumers who are mildly uncomfortable with higher gas prices. The composition of the decline almost certainly reflects the direct household impact of gasoline prices above $4 a gallon, elevated airfares making travel feel inaccessible, and the psychological weight of a six-week-old military conflict with no clear resolution timeline visible to ordinary families watching the news. There's an important distinction to draw between what this sentiment reading means for near-term spending and what it means for the macro trajectory. In the immediate term, consumer spending has been surprisingly resilient even through periods of low sentiment — the pandemic era demonstrated repeatedly that behavioral spending and survey-reported sentiment can diverge significantly when employment remains strong. But sentiment at 47.6 is not a cautionary reading, it's a leading indicator of demand destruction at the margin. If gasoline prices stay elevated through May and June, if the Hormuz situation doesn't resolve, and if airfares keep climbing, the sentiment deterioration will eventually translate into actual spending cuts — particularly in discretionary categories like restaurants, travel, entertainment, and non-essential retail. Claudia Sahm, chief economist at New Century Advisors, described the current environment succinctly as a "whiplash economy" — and that framing captures the essential problem. The supply shock is real, it's painful, and its secondary demand effects are only beginning to manifest in the data. The Fed can look through the headline energy CPI print. It cannot look through a consumer that stops spending.

#### Crude Stays Elevated Despite the Ceasefire — Saudi Arabia Loses 600,000 Barrels Per Day of Production Capacity

WTI Crude is trading at $98.39, up 0.53%, while Brent sits at $96.10, up 0.19%. The ceasefire agreement announced Tuesday bought a two-week pause in U.S.-Iran hostilities — not a resolution, not a permanent agreement, and critically not a reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic through the world's most important energy chokepoint remains minimal. The physical reality of the oil market has not changed because of the ceasefire announcement — it has only changed the probability distribution around future scenarios. And within that adjusted probability distribution, the risk events keep accumulating rather than receding. Saudi Arabia's state press agency disclosed this week that drone strikes on the kingdom's energy infrastructure have reduced its production capacity by approximately 600,000 barrels per day — roughly 10% of normal Saudi crude exports according to Bloomberg's calculations. Separately, strikes on a pumping station serving the East-West pipeline, which Saudi Arabia uses to route oil to Red Sea terminals and bypass the Hormuz choke point, reduced throughput by 700,000 barrels this week. Kuwait separately reported intercepting drone attacks with vital energy facilities among the targeted sites. These are not abstract geopolitical developments — they are direct reductions in the physical supply of crude oil to global markets, and they are happening simultaneously with the Strait of Hormuz operating at minimal capacity. WTI crossed $100 per barrel overnight before pulling back into the high $90s. The technical level of $100 has become both a psychological trigger and a market stress threshold — sustained trading above it would immediately ratchet up the inflationary pressure on April's CPI print and force a reassessment of the "temporary, supply-side" framing the Fed is currently operating under. Oil is not a buy here on a trade basis given the binary weekend risk around Islamabad talks — but the structural floor in crude remains well above $90 as long as Hormuz stays restricted, which makes energy-related hedges and inflation protection assets like gold attractive to hold. Gold at $4,796 is down 0.45% Friday but is on track for its third consecutive weekly gain — a sustained haven bid that reflects genuine uncertainty about whether this ceasefire holds, whether talks succeed, and whether the supply disruption resolves in weeks or months.

#### The Weekend Talks in Islamabad Are the Single Most Important Market Event Between Now and Monday

Every number discussed in this analysis — oil prices, CPI expectations, consumer sentiment, Fed policy odds, equity valuations — flows through one critical variable that will be determined this weekend. JD Vance is leading a U.S. delegation to Islamabad for direct negotiations with Iranian officials over the Strait of Hormuz and the broader terms of the ceasefire. The binary nature of those talks' outcome creates a risk distribution that is genuinely asymmetric. If talks produce a credible pathway toward Hormuz reopening, the oil market reprices lower by potentially $15-20 per barrel, core inflation for April comes in materially softer than current forecasts, consumer sentiment recovers, the S&P 500 gets a clean runway toward recapturing year-to-date losses, and the Fed's probability of cutting rates this year climbs past 50%. That scenario would likely produce one of the strongest single-session equity rallies of the year on Monday morning. If talks collapse or produce no substantive progress, WTI breaks above $100 again on Monday's open, gasoline pump prices head back toward multi-decade highs, the April CPI print becomes catastrophically hot, and the 47.6 consumer sentiment reading starts looking like the leading edge of genuine demand destruction rather than a temporary stress signal. Every equity position, every fixed income trade, and every currency bet in global markets carries weekend gap risk tied to what comes out of Islamabad. Trump's public statement Thursday — warning Iran directly not to charge fees to oil tankers attempting to transit the strait — simultaneously signals Washington's urgency and introduces the risk of Iranian face-saving complications that could stall negotiations. The market is positioned for cautious optimism. It is not positioned for a complete collapse. That asymmetry means the downside is worse than the upside is good from a positioning perspective, and any long position built on the assumption of a clean ceasefire extension carries meaningful stop-loss risk heading into the weekend.

#### The Weekly Scorecard: Best Performance in Months, But Built on Fragile Foundations

The weekly numbers are impressive by any standard. The S&P 500 has gained nearly 4% week-to-date, tracking for its best weekly performance since May. The Nasdaq Composite is up nearly 5% for the week, a move that represents not just a relief rally but a genuine technical recovery of significance. The Dow has added more than 3% week-to-date. The Russell 2000 is up 4.2%, signaling that the rally has had some breadth rather than being purely a large-cap technology phenomenon. Wednesday's session was the detonator for all of this — all three major indexes jumped more than 2% after the ceasefire announcement, with the Dow recording a 1,300-point single-day gain, its best performance since April 2025. But it's worth being precise about what drove this week's recovery. It was not improving economic fundamentals. It was not a resolution of the underlying geopolitical conflict. It was a two-week pause in hostilities that markets chose to interpret as a signal of eventual de-escalation. That's a positioning story, not a fundamental story, and the distinction matters for how durable this rally turns out to be. The S&P 500 has reclaimed its 200-day moving average — the same technical level it broke below in March 2025 ahead of a significant decline — and systematic strategies have been re-engaging on the long side as a result. The last time the index reclaimed the 200-day, it tested it from above and then surged. The technical precedent is bullish, but the macro backdrop today is considerably more complex than it was in that episode.

#### Sector-Level Breakdown: Discretionary Dominates, Energy Struggles to Follow Through

Thursday's sector performance data reinforces the internal bifurcation that's been the defining characteristic of this market all week. Consumer discretionary led all 11 GICS sectors, surging 2.46% — a move driven by the same combination of ceasefire optimism and easing rate cut expectations that is pushing tech higher. Industrials added 1.04%, reflecting some recovery in capital goods and transportation names that had been beaten up on oil cost concerns. Communication services climbed 0.93%. On the losing side, energy fell 1.16% — the worst-performing sector by a meaningful margin — and healthcare slipped 0.19%. The energy sector's underperformance in an environment where crude oil is sitting above $98 per barrel is the most counterintuitive data point in Thursday's tape, and it deserves explanation. Energy producers benefit from high crude prices through expanded margins — but only when they can actually produce and deliver product. Saudi Arabia losing 600,000 barrels per day of production capacity to drone strikes is not a bullish event for integrated oil producers. It's a supply disruption that raises the price of a barrel without proportionally raising the revenue of the companies that would otherwise produce those barrels. Add the operational uncertainty around Red Sea routing, Hormuz transit restrictions, and geopolitical force majeure risk in the region, and the energy sector is caught between high spot prices and genuinely impaired operational predictability. That combination produces a sector that benefits less from the oil price spike than the market might assume, which is exactly what the Thursday performance data reflected. Energy is a HOLD with elevated volatility risk — not because the commodity isn't valuable, but because the ability of individual companies to capture that value amid active infrastructure disruption is deeply uncertain.

#### Asian Markets Confirm the Global Risk Recovery — Nikkei Above 56,900, CSI 300 Surges 1.54%

Overnight session results across Asia-Pacific confirmed that the risk-on impulse from the ceasefire announcement has genuine global traction, not just a U.S.-centric narrative. Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced 1.84% to 56,924.11 — a substantial single-day gain for one of the world's most actively traded equity indexes. The Bank of Japan context matters here: Japan is more directly exposed to elevated oil prices than almost any other major economy, given its near-total dependence on imported crude. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's Friday announcement that Japan will begin releasing 20 days of strategic petroleum reserves starting in May is a direct policy response to the supply shock — and with Japan's total reserve buffer standing at 230 days as of April 6, this release represents a meaningful market signal of intent without creating any reserve depletion risk. The Topix ended essentially flat, reflecting sector-level divergence similar to what U.S. markets are showing. China's CSI 300 surged 1.54% to close at 4,636.57, aided by an economic data point that deserves attention on its own: Chinese factory-gate prices rose for the first time in more than three years. China's producer price index returning to positive territory after an extended deflationary period is a significant macro development — it suggests that domestic demand in China, combined with the global commodity price environment, is generating enough pricing power at the manufacturing level to push PPI above zero. China's CPI rose 1% year-over-year in March, a modest print but directionally consistent with an economy that is gradually escaping the deflationary spiral it has been navigating. The Hang Seng Index finished up 0.47%, not as strong as the CSI 300 but positive. South Korea's Kospi gained 1.40% to close at 5,858.87, with the small-cap Kosdaq adding 1.64% to finish at 1,093.63. India's Nifty 50 and BSE Sensex both rose nearly 1%. Australia's ASX 200 was the lone outlier at -0.31%, likely reflecting its unique commodity export exposure dynamics in an environment where global energy disruption creates complex downstream effects for an economy that exports both energy and mining commodities.

#### European Markets Post Broad Gains Across All Major Bourses

European equity markets extended their recovery on Friday with gains spread across virtually every major index on the continent. The pan-European Stoxx 600 advanced 0.67% to 616.71. Italy's FTSE MIB led the region with a 0.82% gain to 47,717.25, a strong print for one of Europe's more volatile major equity markets. Spain's IBEX 35 added 0.78% to 18,246.90. Germany's DAX climbed 0.51% to 23,927.83 — notable given Germany's direct exposure to energy cost increases through its industrial and manufacturing base. France's CAC 40 advanced 0.44% to 8,282.24. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 gained 0.19% to 10,623.15. British Prime Minister Keir Starmer generated significant political commentary by publicly stating his frustration — he used the word "fed up" explicitly — with energy price volatility driven by the actions of Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin affecting U.K. household energy bills. That statement is diplomatically notable because it represents a sitting head of government from America's closest ally directly and publicly attributing domestic cost-of-living damage to U.S. presidential decisions and Russian geopolitical strategy simultaneously. It also reflects the reality that European energy markets, which had only recently stabilized after the post-2022 Russia-Ukraine energy crisis, are now facing a second energy price shock from a completely different geopolitical source, with no domestic energy security buffer of meaningful scale. Starmer separately called Israel's continued strikes on Lebanon "wrong" — a statement that signals European diplomatic pressure on one of the conflict's secondary theaters is building in a way that could complicate the U.S.-led ceasefire negotiation framework.

#### Treasuries, the Dollar, and Bitcoin Map the Macro Uncertainty

The fixed income and currency markets are telling a story that is slightly less optimistic than the equity tape suggests. The 10-year Treasury yield at 4.31% is up approximately 2 basis points on the session — mild selling in bonds that suggests the market is not fully convinced that the core CPI undershoot today translates into sustained disinflation. The logic is straightforward: today's soft core number is March data. April's print, which will capture the full month of elevated gasoline and jet fuel prices, elevated transportation costs, and secondary effects spreading through the economy, is expected to be materially hotter. Bond investors are discounting that forthcoming data rather than celebrating today's backward-looking number. Yields on the 2-year and 30-year are both moving by similar amounts to the 10-year — roughly 2 basis points each — which indicates a parallel shift in the curve rather than a steepening or flattening signal. A flattening would suggest markets expecting rate cuts relatively soon. A parallel shift means they're adjusting the level of uncertainty across all durations without changing their view on the curve's shape, which is a more neutral-to-cautious fixed income posture. The dollar index is down 0.17% to 95.53, a reaction to the core CPI undershoot and the marginally improved rate cut expectations that followed. A softer dollar is directionally constructive for emerging market assets, for commodity prices denominated in dollars, and for multinational U.S. corporations with international revenue streams. Bitcoin (BTC) is trading at $72,711, up 0.81% on the session. The cryptocurrency continues to occupy an unusual position in the current macro environment — it's simultaneously a risk asset that rallies with equity markets and a non-correlated store of value that attracts capital when sovereign currency dynamics create uncertainty. At $72,711 with 0.81% daily gains against a mixed equity backdrop, Bitcoin is behaving more like a risk asset today than a haven, which is consistent with the broader "less fear" narrative reflected in the VIX's decline to 18.99.

#### Meta Quietly Executes a Legal Containment Strategy While the Stock Moves Higher

Meta Platforms (META) is up 1.01% to $634.74 on the session, a solid day's performance for one of the largest weights in the Nasdaq Composite — and a meaningful contributor to that index's outperformance. But beneath the surface, Meta is executing a legal containment strategy that the market is watching but not yet fully pricing as an ongoing risk. Meta is actively pulling Facebook and Instagram ads that had been running to recruit new plaintiffs for social media addiction litigation — a category of lawsuit that has been building for years and has now produced two significant adverse verdicts in rapid succession. A Los Angeles jury found Meta and Alphabet's Google (GOOGL) jointly liable in a case involving a young woman's depression and suicidal ideation, awarding $6 million in combined damages. A separate New Mexico jury ordered Meta specifically to pay $375 million after finding that the company had misled users about product safety for young users and had enabled the sexual exploitation of children on its platforms. Those two verdicts represent a combined $381 million in awarded damages from just two cases. The scale of the litigation pipeline makes those numbers look small by comparison to potential exposure: more than 3,300 addiction-related lawsuits are currently pending in California state court alone against Meta, Google, Snap, and ByteDance. Another 2,400 individual, municipal, state, and school district lawsuits have been consolidated in California federal court. Pulling plaintiff recruitment ads is a sensible legal defense tactic — it reduces the active pipeline of new litigants without affecting existing cases — but it also represents an implicit acknowledgment that the litigation exposure is significant enough to warrant proactive management at the marketing level. META is a HOLD at current prices. The underlying business and advertising platform performance remain strong, but the litigation tail risk is a multi-year overhang that individual adverse verdicts will keep bringing back into focus. At $634 with a $375 million verdict already on the books and thousands of cases pending, the discount rate applied to Meta's earnings needs to incorporate the probability of cumulative litigation costs that dwarf anything currently in consensus estimates.

#### NVDA, AVGO, MRVL — The Semiconductor Trade Thesis Gets Bank of America Validation

Beyond TSMC's print, the semiconductor sector received institutional validation from Bank of America analyst Vivek Arya, who raised his 2026 global semiconductor revenue target to $1.3 trillion. The explicit call-outs in Arya's note are NVIDIA (NVDA), Broadcom (AVGO), and Marvell (MRVL) as the primary beneficiaries of the AI-driven compute, networking, and memory spending wave. NVDA is up 1.9% to $187.44, consistent with its role as the index weight and sentiment driver for the entire AI hardware complex. Gartner confirmed the $1.3 trillion figure independently, calling 2026 the third consecutive year of double-digit semiconductor revenue growth. Within four years, the industry is projected to reach $2 trillion — a 20% compound growth rate versus the historical norm of 8-10%. The delta between those two numbers is the AI premium, and it's being validated by real enterprise spending rather than speculative forward projections. Data center capex from hyperscalers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta — has not meaningfully slowed despite energy cost pressures, geopolitical uncertainty, and rate volatility. That spending persistence is the single most important bullish data point in the technology sector, and TSMC's Q1 revenue record is the clearest confirmation of it available to the market right now. NVDA, AVGO, and TSM are all BUY on any meaningful pullback. The AI buildout is a multi-year capital deployment cycle that is demonstrably more durable than macro disruptions in the $90-100 oil range, and the companies positioned at the critical constraint points in that buildout — advanced node silicon, networking silicon, optical interconnect — are the clearest expression of that durability.

# The Great Rebalancing: How the 'Silicon to Steel' Rotation Reshaped Markets in Q1 2026

Published at April 13th 2026, 10:06 AM EDT via MarketMinute

ⓘ This article is third-party content and does not represent the views of this site. We make no guarantees regarding its accuracy or completeness.

The first quarter of 2026 has marked a historic regime shift in global financial markets, bringing a definitive end to the unbridled "AI Gold Rush" that defined the mid-2020s. As investors fled high-multiple technology giants in favor of "real economy" sectors like energy, industrials, and value-oriented staples, the market witnessed a violent internal rotation. By the close of March, the technology-heavy NASDAQ Composite (INDEXNASDAQ:.IXIC) had plummeted 7%, while the broader S&P 500 (INDEXSP:.INX) slid 4%, masking a massive surge in the energy and industrial sectors.

This transition—now being dubbed the "Great Rebalancing"—represents more than just a seasonal correction. It is a fundamental repricing of risk as the "higher-for-longer" interest rate environment of the Federal Reserve collided with a geopolitical energy shock and a growing skepticism regarding the immediate return on investment (ROI) of generative artificial intelligence. For the first time in years, the "Magnificent Seven" have lost their crown as the market’s primary engine, replaced by the humming turbines of power utilities and the drill bits of domestic oil producers.

## The Perfect Storm: Geopolitics and Valuation Fatigue

The timeline leading to the Q1 2026 shift began in late February, when military escalations in the Middle East led to the temporary closure of the Strait of Hormuz. With 20% of the world’s oil supply suddenly under threat, Brent crude prices surged past $110 per barrel, reigniting inflationary fears that many had hoped were buried in 2024. This "energy-driven inflation" effectively trapped the Federal Reserve, which maintained the federal funds rate at a restrictive 3.50% to 3.75%, crushing hopes for the aggressive spring rate cuts that tech investors had already priced into their models.

Simultaneously, the market narrative surrounding Artificial Intelligence shifted from speculative hype to "margin mandates." After three years of massive capital expenditure (CapEx) on data centers and chips, institutional investors began demanding tangible productivity gains. When several Tier-1 software firms reported stagnant seat growth despite record AI spending in February earnings calls, the "AI CapEx Trap" narrative took hold. This led to a "multiple compression" event, where investors were no longer willing to pay 40 times earnings for growth that seemed increasingly deferred, triggering a massive liquidity flight into cash-flow-heavy value stocks.

The reaction was swift and clinical. By mid-March, the "HALO" trade—Heavy Assets, Low Obsolescence—became the dominant strategy on Wall Street. Investment shifted toward companies that provide the physical infrastructure of the modern world: power, machinery, and fuel. While the tech sector saw its worst quarterly performance since 2022, the Energy Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLE) posted gains of over 12%, highlighting a market that has rediscovered its appetite for "tangible" earnings over "digital" promises.

## Winners and Losers of the New Regime

The rotation has created a stark divide between the "Frictionless" digital world and the "Friction" world of physical assets. Among the primary beneficiaries is ExxonMobil (NYSE:XOM), which saw its stock price climb nearly 28% in the first quarter. Leveraging its 2024 acquisition of Pioneer Natural Resources, Exxon captured massive upstream margins as oil prices stayed elevated. Similarly, Chevron Corporation (NYSE:CVX) gained 30%, as its focus on the Permian Basin and Guyana provided a "safe haven" from Middle Eastern supply disruptions.

In the industrial sector, Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT) emerged as an unexpected "AI play," rising 25% year-to-date. As the physical build-out of data centers required massive amounts of backup power and construction equipment, Caterpillar’s $51 billion backlog became a beacon for value investors. NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE) also benefited, gaining 11% as the "Golden Age of Power Demand" took hold, with AI data centers consuming electricity at rates comparable to entire industrialized nations.

Conversely, the tech titans faced a reckoning. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) endured its worst quarter since 2008, dropping 23.4% as investors questioned its $38 billion quarterly AI spend. Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) fell 12.7%, hamstrung by the 2025 repeal of federal EV tax credits and a saturated global market. Even the indomitable Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) lagged the broader market, as a lack of a "breakout" AI consumer device led many to treat the stock as a source of funds for the rotation into energy and small-caps.

## A Return to Fundamentals and Policy Shifts

The Q1 2026 shift mirrors the 2000 Dot-com crash in its "valuation exhaustion," but carries the macro-economic weight of the 2022 inflationary shock. Historically, such rotations signal a "healthy normalization"—a transition from a momentum-driven market to a fundamental-driven one. This shift has been accelerated by the "One Big Beautiful Bill" Act (OBBBA) of 2025, which pivoted federal support toward "baseload" power like nuclear and natural gas, providing a long-term tailwind for traditional energy firms at the expense of speculative "green tech" and software ventures.

Regulatory pressure has also played a role. With the United States v. Google (NASDAQ:GOOGL) antitrust rulings imposing "behavioral" constraints on big tech’s data monopolies, and the imminent EU AI Act increasing compliance costs, the "moats" around Silicon Valley are beginning to look more like expensive liabilities. This has leveled the playing field for specialized "Physical AI" companies—those integrating automation into domestic manufacturing and mining—who are less affected by the digital antitrust landscape.

The broader significance lies in the "Silicon to Steel" narrative. The market is signaling that the next phase of economic growth will not be driven by software eating the world, but by the physical resources required to run that software. Competition has moved from who has the best Large Language Model (LLM) to who controls the copper, the lithium, and the gigawatts.

## Looking Ahead: The "Physical Execution" Era

In the short term, the market remains vulnerable to further volatility as the "higher-for-longer" rate environment settles in. However, the pivot to value creates significant opportunities for active managers who had been sidelined during the passive, tech-led bull run of 2023-2025. We expect to see a surge in M&A activity within the industrial and energy sectors as cash-rich firms look to consolidate their grip on the supply chains of the future.

The long-term challenge for Tech giants will be "AI Monetization 2.0." Companies like NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA), which saw flat performance in Q1 2026 despite strong earnings, will need to prove that their chips are creating actual economic surplus for their customers, not just participating in a circular CapEx economy. We may see a strategic pivot toward "Physical AI"—the integration of intelligence into robotics and logistics—as software-only solutions face diminishing marginal returns and increased regulatory scrutiny.

## The Investor’s Roadmap for 2026

The key takeaway from Q1 2026 is that the "passive" era of buying the S&P 500 and letting tech do the heavy lifting is, for now, over. The market has transitioned into a "cyclical value" phase where dividends, free cash flow, and tangible assets are the primary drivers of alpha. Investors should brace for a period where "Old Economy" stocks act as the new defensive core of their portfolios.

As we move into the second half of 2026, the watchwords will be "energy security" and "infrastructure ROI." Watch for the performance of equal-weighted indices over cap-weighted ones, as they will more accurately reflect the broadening of this market. While the decline in the major indices may feel painful, it represents a necessary re-coupling of stock prices with the physical reality of the global economy—a shift that may provide a more stable, albeit slower-growing, foundation for the years to come.

# Dow Jones closes lower as markets digest inflation shock and mixed tech action

Last updated: 16:15 10 Apr 2026 EDT, First published: 08:00 10 Apr 2026 EDT

### 4.15pm: Stocks see second week of gains

US stocks finished Friday’s session mixed as investors reacted to new inflation data ahead of key peace talks this weekend between the US and Iran.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq ended the day higher up 0.4% at 22,90, while the Dow Jones fell 0.6% to 47,916 points, and the S&P 500 was down 0.1% at 6,816 points. However, all three indexes finished the week higher, marking a second straight week of gains.

### 3:45pm: Proactive news headlines

- Listen
- Digi Power X Inc entered an updated agreement to raise up to $75 million through an at-the-market equity program as it pivots toward AI data centers and GPU-as-a-Service.
- Century Lithium Corp promoted Todd Fayram to chief technical officer to support advancing its Angel Island project and broader technical strategy.
- Mkango Resources Ltd shares rose after it raised £12.5 million to fund a potential German acquisition and expand processing operations.

### 2:45pm: Market movers

- ServiceNow Inc was downgraded by UBS to Neutral as confidence in its AI leadership weakens amid rising budget pressure on non-AI software spending.
- CoreWeave shares surged after securing a multi-year deal with Anthropic to provide large-scale cloud infrastructure for its Claude AI models.
- Software stocks broadly declined as investor चिंता grows that rapid advances in AI—highlighted by developments at Anthropic—could disrupt long-term earnings across the sector.
- Mkango Resources Ltd shares climbed after it raised £12.5 million to fund a potential German acquisition and expand processing capacity.
- Mercantile Ports and Logistics shares jumped sharply as it moved to repay all debt and pursue legal action to reclaim its Karanja terminal in India.
- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co beat forecasts with strong revenue growth driven by AI demand, reinforcing confidence in the ongoing AI investment cycle.

### 1:20pm: Equities managing to hold on

Gina Bolvin, President of Bolvin Wealth Management Group, said equities are still managing to hold onto this week’s gains despite higher oil prices, rising geopolitical tensions, and a fragile ceasefire backdrop, underscoring what she described as continued market resilience.

"There’s a growing disconnect between the headlines and market behavior. Bad news isn’t triggering the same kind of selling pressure, which tells you positioning is shifting," Bolvin said.

"If the market can close positive today—and more importantly, hold into the weekend—that’s a strong signal. Recently, investors haven’t wanted that kind of exposure. A change there would say confidence is quietly rebuilding beneath the surface."

### 12:20pm: Software stocks get hit

Software stocks traded lower on Friday amid mounting investor concerns about how rapidly advancing artificial intelligence (AI) could reshape the sector’s long-term earnings outlook, extending a broader AI-driven slump.

Leading software stocks lower on Friday was Cloudflare (NYSE:NET), which was down 12.6%.

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc (NASDAQ:CRWD) was down 7.2%, SentinelOne (NYSE:S) fell 5.5%, Zscaler Inc. (NASDAQ:ZS) was down 5.1%, Okta Inc (NASDAQ:OKTA) was down 5%, and Intuit Inc (NASDAQ:INTU, XETRA:ITU) lost 4%.

Salesforce Inc (NYSE:CRM, XETRA:FOO) stock fell 3.2%, Adobe Inc (NASDAQ:ADBE) was down 2.3%, Atlassian (NASDAQ:TEAM) fell 2.1%, and SAP (NYSE:SAP) was down about 1%.

The S&P 500 Software & Services index is down more than 26% in the year to date, trading at about $3,950.

### 11:05am: Fed 'clearly on hold'

Declines in medical care and used vehicle prices in March point to some easing in inflation pressures, according to Jeffrey Roach of LPL Financial, but he noted that he would need to see sustained moderation in health care costs before becoming more confident that inflation will return to the Federal Reserve’s 2% target by next year.

"Since the Hormuz chokepoint was closed for an extended period, we should expect another one or two hot inflation prints, driven by transportation services and some durable goods categories," Roach commented following today's CPI print.

"The second order effects will likely add another 0.2 over the next few months. The Fed clearly is on hold for the next several meetings."

### 10:00am: Mixed start

Markets are off to a mixed start on Friday as investors digest a fresh inflation surprise and a pullback in tech names following renewed concerns around AI-driven software disruption.

The Nasdaq Composite is up 0.4%, while the S&P 500 edges just 0.1% higher. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, meanwhile, is down 0.3%, giving back some of its recent momentum.

The mood follows a strong run earlier in the week, with the S&P 500 now attempting to secure its first positive Friday since February 20 after seven consecutive days of gains.

On the macro side, inflation came in hotter than expected, leaving analysts weighing what the print means for the outlook ahead. Jamie Cox, managing partner at Harris Financial Group, noted that the March data may understate the full impact of the oil shock. “While I'm glad to see the effects to be less than expected in March, the effects in April are now more likely to be worse,” Harris cautioned.

In equities, pressure is building in parts of the software and AI-adjacent trade after concerns emerged around autonomous AI agents. Cloudflare is down 11%, Snowflake is off 7.5%, and ServiceNow has fallen 6.7%, weighing on the broader tech complex.

### 8:50am: Inflation rises but energy prices surge

The consumer price index came in slightly cooler than expected in March, though a sharp increase in energy prices highlighted ongoing volatility in the data.

CPI rose 3.3% year-over-year, just below expectations of 3.4%, while monthly inflation matched forecasts with a 0.9% increase.

Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, also came in slightly below expectations. Core CPI rose 2.6% annually versus forecasts of 2.7%, and increased 0.2% month-over-month, compared with expectations of a 0.3% gain.

However, energy costs surged during the month. The energy index jumped 10.9%, marking the largest increase since 2005. Gasoline prices were a key driver, with the gas price index rising 21.2%.

### 8am: Caution prevails

US equity futures point to a broadly flat open, with a marginally positive tone belying the cautious mood across global markets. All eyes turn to the March CPI print, due at 8:30am ET, which is expected to reflect the inflationary ripple effects of elevated energy prices.

The S&P 500 is set to open 0.1% higher, headed for an eighth day of gains. The Nasdaq Composite is seen rising 0.2%, while futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average are up 4 points.

Markets closed higher on Thursday, with tech leading the way as investors looked past geopolitical tensions and focused on the upcoming inflation data. The Nasdaq climbed 0.8%, the S&P 500 rose 0.6%, and the Dow Jones also gained 0.6%.

In Europe, markets are trading higher this morning. London's FTSE 100 is up 0.3, while Paris is 0.9% firmer and Frankfurt has gained 0.8%

AJ Bell's head of markets, Dan Coatsworth, said geopolitical uncertainty continues to weigh on sentiment, describing the recently announced ceasefire as feeling "fragile at times," though he noted that reports of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approving direct talks with Lebanon could prove a constructive development in resolving one of the key sticking points between the parties.

March CPI, forecast at 3.3%, the highest reading since May 2024, is expected to have been driven largely by higher fuel prices, one of the most immediate economic transmission channels of geopolitical conflict.

Coatsworth flagged that markets may look through the headline number, with greater scrutiny likely on the core reading, which strips out food and energy, to assess whether inflationary pressures are broadening into the wider economy.

- Technical traders monitor XLK XLK--(tech) and XTN (transport) for rotation signals, with volume profiles and 50-day moving averages indicating potential structural shifts in market leadership.

The leadership hierarchy has flipped. For three years, tech dragged the S&P 500 higher. This year, energy, materials, and industrials are crushing it-while tech stumbles.

Energy stocks lead the charge, with XLE XLE-- up 21.5% this year. Materials follows at +17.6%, and industrials at +12.3%. By contrast, technology is down 3% for 2026. That's a dramatic reversal from the narrative most investors have built their portfolios around.

Here's what's happening under the hood: supply and demand is shifting in real time. The overcrowded AI trade has reached capacity. Investors have piled into hyperscalers and the Magnificent Seven for years-now they're rotating out. The Magnificent Seven ETF is down 8.8% so far in 2026, a stark contrast to the sector's recent dominance.

The 1-year return numbers still show tech strong- XLK at 27.89% and IYW at 28.22%-but those figures are carrying 2025's gains. The current-year story is different. Price action doesn't lie: buyers have moved on.

What's driving the rotation? Three factors. First, AI fatigue has set in-investors are questioning the ROI on the AI buildout. Second, industrials are benefiting from the physical infrastructure demand regardless of who wins the AI race. Third, energy is surging on geopolitical tailwinds-Venezuelan oil reserves and U.S.-Iran tensions are fueling crude prices.

For the technical trader, this is a classic rotation setup. The question isn't whether tech will recover-it's whether the leadership change is structural or cyclical. The volume and price action suggest something meaningful is shifting under the market's feet.

## Semiconductor Fundamentals: The AI Boom Still Driving Revenue

The semiconductor industry is riding an unprecedented revenue wave in 2026, with projections ranging from $975 billion to $1.3 trillion in annual sales. Growth is accelerating-26% projected for 2026 after 22% in 2025-fueling a confidence index at 63, the third-highest reading in two decades. Ninety-three percent of industry executives expect revenue growth. On paper, this is a trader's dream: strong fundamentals, clear momentum, and a bullish consensus.

But the price action tells a more nuanced story.

The AI boom is driving roughly half of total chip revenue while representing less than 0.2% of total unit volume. That's the structural paradox at the heart of the sector. AI chips-particularly high-bandwidth memory and accelerators-are commanding massive prices. Memory prices alone are surging 125% this year. But this is a high-value, low-volume game. The industry is selling fewer chips at much higher prices, not moving more units.

That distinction matters for the technical trader. When you have 50% of revenue concentrated in a sliver of the product mix, you have a concentration risk that's baked into the sector's valuation. The top three chip stocks now account for 80% of the combined market cap of the top ten. The market has already priced in the AI thesis-aggressively.

The confidence index at 63 reflects that enthusiasm. But it also masks emerging fractures. For the first time, semiconductor leaders rank tariffs and trade policy as their top concern-not AI demand slowdown. Energy procurement for advanced manufacturing facilities is ranking alongside geopolitical risk. These aren't hypotheticals; they're operational headwinds that could materialize before the 2026 earnings cycle completes.

From a supply-demand perspective, the question is whether the current price strength discounts future fundamentals or whether there's more room to run. The volume profile suggests the former-market cap has grown 46% in a single year while silicon-wafer shipments increased only 5.4%. The disconnect between revenue growth and physical production growth is widening.

For traders watching for rotation signals, the semiconductor sector presents a classic tension: fundamentals remain strong, but the market has already priced perfection. Any crack in the AI demand story-or escalation in tariff/energy risks-could trigger a swift re-rating. The setup favors caution on new long exposure at these levels, with tight stops if holding positions. The fundamentals justify the price, but they also justify the risk.

## Transportation/Logistics: Structural Tailwinds or Overstated?

The transportation sector is fighting two battles at once: recovering margins from years of disruption while navigating a world where global trade is losing its share of GDP growth. For the technical trader, the question is whether the fundamentals support continued leadership-or whether this is a sector running on fumes.

The industry has spent the past several years navigating one of the most volatile periods in modern supply chain history. What's emerged is a sector focused on end-to-end productivity and margin recovery. But here's the catch: global trade is playing a smaller role in GDP across major economies, with growth projected to modestly slow in 2026. That's not a tailwind-it's a headwind.

AI adoption is improving efficiency-route optimization, autonomous decision-making, inventory management-but tariff challenges remain the key risk. The sector's confidence is built on operational improvements, not demand expansion.

The freight markets tell the real story. Ocean freight is facing overcapacity with rates down 20% year-over-year-carriers are looking at a combined $10 billion loss. That's not a minor blip; that's a structural pressure that will take time to work through the system. Air freight is doing better, with demand growing approximately 2.7% in 2026, but that's modest growth driven largely by high-tech shipments and AI infrastructure-narrow demand, not broad-based.

For the technical trader, the setup is clear: watch XTN's relative strength against the S&P 500. If the sector is truly leading, it should hold up or outperform during market pullbacks. Look for volume spikes on up days-those are the moments when institutional buyers are stepping in. If volume dries up on rallies and increases on declines, that's the market telling you the fundamentals aren't supporting the price.

The bottom line: transportation has margin recovery as a tailwind, but trade slowdown and freight overcapacity are powerful headwinds. This isn't a sector I'd chase at these levels without confirmation that buyers are still accumulating. The fundamentals are mixed, and in a rotation environment, mixed fundamentals mean mixed price action.

## Technical Setup: Key Levels and What to Watch

For the technical trader, the sector rotation story translates into specific price action setups. Here's what to monitor.

XLK: Breakout or Breakdown?

Technology is down 3% YTD as measured by XLK-the first sector in the S&P 500 to post negative returns this year. That weakness has compressed price into a consolidation range. The question for traders: can buyers muster enough force to break above recent highs, or does this signal deeper structural weakness?

Watch the 50-day moving average as critical support. A clean breakout above the consolidation ceiling on high volume would signal fresh institutional accumulation and could reignite the tech rally. But if XLK XLK-- breaks below that moving average with expanding volume on the decline, it confirms the rotation is accelerating-not pausing.

XTN: Relative Strength Under Fire

The transportation sector faces a tougher test. With trade growth slowing and ocean freight rates down 20% year-over-year, XTN needs to demonstrate relative strength against the S&P 500 to maintain leadership. I'm looking for volume spikes on up days-those are the moments when buyers are stepping in with conviction. If volume dries up during rallies and expands during declines, the sector's fundamentals aren't supporting the price.

The Key Risk: Semiconductor Failure

Here's the scenario that keeps me up at night: if semiconductor stocks fail to hold current levels, the broader market could see a swift rotation out of tech entirely. The sector's confidence index sits at 63-elevated but vulnerable, and any crack in the AI demand story could trigger a re-rating. I'm watching for pullbacks that hold above key support levels. If semis break down with volume, it's a signal to reduce tech exposure immediately.

Volume Profile: Where the Money Is

The volume profile reveals where institutional buyers are active. Look for high-volume nodes at current price levels-those are the zones where supply and demand are in equilibrium. A breakout above these nodes on heavy volume confirms genuine accumulation. A break below signals distribution.

Overbought/Oversold Signals

Several tech names are trading well above their 200-day moving averages-technically overbought. In a rotation environment, these names are vulnerable to sharp pullbacks. Conversely, sectors like energy and materials that have run hard may be due for consolidation. The key is watching for divergence: price making new highs while momentum indicators fail to confirm. That's often the earliest warning of a rotation in progress.

The AI stocks that drove three consecutive years of outsized market gains have gone flat in 2026 while the energy sector is up nearly 30 percent, as the Iran war’s energy shock has forced a sector rotation that is rewriting the portfolio playbook investors relied on through 2024 and 2025.

Summary

- Best Picks
- The S&P 500 and Nasdaq are both roughly flat in 2026 after both indexes gained more than 40 percent in the prior two years, while energy stocks are up nearly 30 percent and consumer staples have risen more than 7 percent, with the Iran war driving oil above $100 and making energy the dominant return source in the market this year.
- Investors are rotating out of AI infrastructure plays and into energy, defense, and dividend stocks, with Nvidia down approximately 17 percent from its highs and Palantir off more than 30 percent from its November peak, while Motley Fool analysis describes the shift as a “great rotation” that is likely temporary but has already lasted long enough to require genuine portfolio repositioning.
- The same Iran war driving energy sector gains is also pressuring AI stocks through two channels: elevated oil keeps inflation high, which suppresses rate cut expectations and tightens the liquidity conditions that growth stocks require, and rising energy costs increase the operating expenses of the AI data centers that the sector’s capital spending programs depend on.

As Motley Fool’s April 13 analysis concluded, “it’s clear that the recipe that led to riches in 2024 and 2025 doesn’t work for 2026.” The piece identifies three factors investors need to hold simultaneously: maintain tech exposure for the eventual bounce, add energy and consumer diversification for current conditions, and accept that the AI infrastructure thesis has not changed even if the near-term stock performance has. The International Energy Agency projects that AI data center electricity consumption will grow 15 percent per year through 2030, more than four times faster than total electricity demand, meaning energy and AI are structurally linked even as they trade in opposite directions right now.

# AI Stocks: Why the Rotation Into Energy Is Logical Rather Than Permanent

The Iran war has done something that valuation concerns and ROI skepticism could not accomplish on their own: it gave investors a near-term alternative to AI stocks with real upside. Energy stocks do not require a multi-year payoff thesis. They produce higher earnings directly when oil prices rise, making them straightforward beneficiaries of the exact macro environment that is suppressing growth stock valuations. The rotation is rational given the current conditions, but it is also inherently self-limiting. The war will end. Oil will come down. When it does, the liquidity conditions that support growth stocks return with it, and the earnings growth projections that made AI infrastructure plays attractive in 2024 will not have changed.

You might also like: Crypto market splits as RaveDAO soars 200% while Polkadot, Zcash slide

## What the Energy Surge Means for Crypto Markets

The energy sector’s 30 percent gain in 2026 is directly tied to the same oil shock that has been the primary bitcoin macro headwind since February. Bitcoin has traded as a high-beta risk asset through the entire Iran conflict, selling when oil spikes and recovering on ceasefire news. The pattern shows an 85 percent correlation between bitcoin and the Nasdaq during energy price surges, meaning the same macro conditions suppressing AI stocks are also suppressing crypto.

## What Investors Are Watching for a Signal to Rotate Back

The signals that would reverse the rotation are the same ones the crypto market is watching: ceasefire extension or war resolution, oil back below $90, and a Fed that can credibly discuss rate cuts again. Motley Fool’s analysis notes that technology is “too important a sector to be down for the long term” and that pulling money out of tech entirely means forfeiting the eventual bounce, which has historically been sharp after extended underperformance driven by external macro shocks rather than deteriorating fundamentals.
