# Chips and Electrons: How the Semiconductor Trade Became an Energy Trade

12 min read

May 13, 2026

--

Share

The semiconductor sector has always moved in cycles, but the cycle has changed. The chips that used to compete for shelf space inside a PC now compete for megawatts on a substation. This is a walk through how chip stocks correlate with each other, how investors price that correlation, and why the energy sector — once an unrelated trade — is now the constraint that gates the entire stack.

## Part I — The Past: When Chips Were Just Chips

For most of its history, the semiconductor industry was a textbook cyclical. Demand surged, fabs over-built, prices collapsed, capacity was idled, and the cycle reset. Between major downcycles, the gap was typically three to four years. Memory was the most violent — Micron’s stock swung through 70–80% drawdowns more than once. Logic was slightly more forgiving but still bound by the same physics: capacity comes online with an 18-to-24-month lag, demand turns on a dime.

## The Dot-Com Pattern (1995–2002)

The closest historical analog to today is the dot-com era — but the analogy is more instructive when you look at what was different, not just what rhymes.

In the late 1990s, telecom and internet infrastructure drove a chip boom. Cisco, Intel, Qualcomm, and Oracle became the “Four Horsemen” of the rally. Telecom capex peaked at roughly $121 billion in 2000 (about $213B in today’s dollars) — a single-cycle capital deployment that, until recently, had no peer. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) traded at a price-to-book of 8.8x at the June 2000 peak. Cisco hit a P/E of 472. Intel, the bellwether, was priced as if its dominance would compound forever.

What broke the trade was not a single catalyst but a sequence:

1. MicroStrategy’s revenue restatement (March 2000) — the first crack in earnings credibility.
2. Intel’s September 2000 revenue warning — the stock fell 40% in a single day, dragging the entire supply chain with it.
3. VC funding dried up — venture capital had peaked at $112.3B in 2000; the IPO market froze; downstream demand evaporated.

By October 2002, the NASDAQ was down 78% from its peak. The SOX fell 82% peak to trough. Cisco lost 80% of its market cap.

## What the Old Correlation Framework Looked Like

In the pre-AI era, chip stocks correlated tightly with each other (driven by shared end-market exposure) but loosely with the broader economy. The correlation matrix looked roughly like this:

Sector pair Correlation regime Semis ↔ Semis High (0.7–0.9) — shared cycle Semis ↔ Industrials Low (0.2–0.4) — different drivers Semis ↔ Utilities Near zero — utilities were a defensive bond proxy Semis ↔ Energy (oil & gas) Slightly negative — energy was an input cost

The reason matters: chip demand was driven by units shipped (PCs, phones, autos), and unit volumes were a downstream effect of consumer and enterprise capex. Power was an operating cost, not a strategic input. A fab in Hsinchu cared about water and clean rooms; a data center in Ashburn cared about latency to NYSE. Neither was bottlenecked on the grid.

That world is gone.

## Part II — The Present: One Trade, Three Sectors

The 2024–2026 AI buildout has done something the previous bull cycles never managed: it has collapsed three historically independent sectors — semiconductors, industrials, and utilities — into a single correlated trade, with hyperscaler capital expenditure as the shared input.

The headline number is striking. The 45-day correlation between the S&P 500 Industrial Sector and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index has climbed to 0.75 — the highest reading in more than two years and approaching levels that historically only show up during macro shocks (2008, COVID), not during sector rallies. Vertiv, Eaton, Caterpillar, and Cummins all carry correlations above 60% with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF.

This is not a coincidence. It is a structural reflection of where the money is flowing.

## The Chip Ecosystem in 2026

Start with the chip stack itself. Five names dominate the AI trade, and they are not interchangeable:

NVIDIA sits at the center. FY2026 revenue closed at $215.9B, up 65% year-over-year, with data center revenue at $194B (up 68%). Q4 FY26 alone came in at $68.1B. The platform moat — CUDA, NVLink, the software stack — keeps multiples in the 30–32x forward earnings range with 48 buy ratings and zero sells across covered analysts. The next-gen Rubin architecture is in the channel, though TrendForce has trimmed its 2026 high-end GPU share estimate from 29% to 22% on supply tuning issues.

TSMC is the foundry that physically builds everything NVIDIA, AMD, Broadcom, and Apple design. 2025 revenue of $122.9B (up 31.6%), HPC at 58% of revenue, operating margins of 58.1%. Trading at roughly 24x forward earnings, it is meaningfully cheaper than NVIDIA or Broadcom — the discount priced in is Taiwan geopolitical risk plus FX. Capex of NT$350.76B last quarter alone, with the first U.S. Blackwell wafer rolling off the Arizona line.

Broadcom has moved up the stack on custom AI silicon. AI semi revenue projected to exceed $30B in FY2026, with VMware adding a high-margin software cushion. The trade-off is valuation — roughly 41x forward earnings, the most expensive of the three, leaving little margin for execution slips.

AMD is the most volatile of the bunch. Q1 2026 revenue of $10.25B with data center sales up 57% YoY. Q2 guidance of ~$11.2B beat consensus; 20+ brokerages raised price targets in a week. Management’s stated five-year target is 60%+ CAGR for the data center segment. The bull case is real; the question is whether ROCm software adoption can sustain the share-take story.

Micron rounds out the top four in the PHLX index. Posted its strongest five-day performance in 16 years (+30%) as HBM demand from AI accelerators tightened. Note that HBM base dies are themselves packaged at TSMC — yet another tie back to the foundry.

Behind them sit ASML (EUV lithography monopoly), Applied Materials and Lam Research (deposition and etch), and the broader equipment cohort.

## Why They Move Together

The PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) is up 175% over three years and reportedly up 65% year-to-date in 2026. This is not breadth — this is concentration. The top four constituents (NVIDIA, Broadcom, Micron, AMD) drive most of the move. NVIDIA alone is 19.37% of SMH (the most-traded semi ETF); TSMC is 11.59%; Broadcom 7.67%.

The correlation between these names has tightened because they share a single demand input: hyperscaler capex. When Alphabet announces $175–185B in 2026 capex (with $70–74B specifically for data centers), every name in the chip stack reprices simultaneously, because they all sit on the same bill of materials. Microsoft is committing $80B+ in FY2026. Meta is on track for $80–100B. Combined, the four largest hyperscalers will spend more than $300B annually on data center infrastructure in 2026, and the broader IEA-tracked figure for the top five tech companies’ total capex hit $400B in 2025 and is projected to rise 75% in 2026.

That is the cleanest correlation driver the chip sector has ever had. The trade is no longer “PC cycle” or “smartphone cycle.” It is “the four buyers.”

## The Industrial Bridge

Here is where it gets interesting for anyone modeling the trade. The same capex flow that buys GPUs also buys generators, switchgear, transformers, busways, and cooling.

Look at the Q1 2026 data:

- Caterpillar: Total revenue $17.42B (+22% YoY). The blowout came from Energy & Transportation — large generator sets and turbines for data centers surged.
- GE Vernova: Q1 electrification orders from data centers exceeded all of 2025 combined. Backlog expected to reach $200B by end of 2026.
- Vertiv (cooling, power management): Q1 net sales +30% YoY; raised full-year guidance to ~$13.75B.
- Quanta Services (transmission/grid contractor): Record backlog of $48.5B as utilities expand to meet projected loads.
- Eaton (electrical equipment): tracking near-record orders on data center power distribution.

These are the names that used to trade on construction cycles and oil-and-gas capex. Now their order books are dictated by NVIDIA’s GTC keynote and Microsoft’s capex guidance. Wolfe Research’s May 11 warning was explicit: power supply constraints, raw material shortages, and regulatory bottlenecks could slow the AI buildout — and that would hit both semis and industrials simultaneously, because they are now the same trade.

## The Energy Linkage

The third leg is the one nobody priced two years ago: power generation. The numbers explain why.

The IEA estimates global data center electricity consumption was ~415 TWh in 2024 (about 1.5% of world total), growing at a 12% CAGR since 2017 — four times faster than overall electricity demand. By 2026, that figure could approach 1,050 TWh, which would make data centers, if they were a country, the fifth-largest electricity consumer in the world. The IEA’s base case has data center demand reaching 945 TWh by 2030, 1,200 TWh by 2035.

BloombergNEF’s forecast is more aggressive: ~400 TWh in 2024 climbing to 1,600 TWh by 2034 — a 4x increase. Morgan Stanley projects U.S. data center demand alone hitting 74 GW by 2028, with a 49 GW shortfall in available power access. U.S. utility capex on AI-related infrastructure is projected at $1.4 trillion through 2028 and rising.

This is what has dragged the regulated utilities into the AI trade. Names that historically traded as bond proxies — yield plays for retirees — are suddenly growth stocks. Constellation Energy posted 2025 revenue of $25.5B (+8.3% YoY) running 21 reactors across 12 sites, the largest nuclear fleet in the U.S. The company has 2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $11.00–$12.00, raised buybacks to $5B, and has $3.9B earmarked for capacity uprates.

The marquee deals are now well-known but worth listing in one place:

Deal Counterparty Capacity Timing Microsoft — Constellation (Three Mile Island restart / “Crane Clean Energy Center”) Microsoft 835 MW 20-year PPA, restart 2027 Meta — Constellation (Illinois nuclear) Meta 1.1 GW 20-year, begins 2027 AWS — Talen Energy (Susquehanna) Amazon 1,920 MW Through 2042, extension option Vistra — Meta (Comanche Peak + PJM fleet) Meta 2.1 GW Long-term, includes 300 MW SMR option Meta — Oklo (Pike County, OH) Meta 1.2 GW 16 Aurora reactors @ 75 MW, first units ~2030 Amazon — X-energy / Energy Northwest Amazon 5+ GW SMR pipeline Initial deployments late 2020s Google — Kairos Power Google 500 MW fleet Hermes 2 online 2030, full fleet 2035 Oracle — three SMRs (announced) Oracle ~1 GW Mid-2030s

That table is, in effect, a new correlation matrix. Each one of those PPAs ties a hyperscaler’s chip demand to a specific generation asset. When the chip stack reprices, the power stack reprices the same week. When Constellation files an 8-K on a new uprate, NVIDIA bulls notice — because that megawatt is a constraint on inference capacity 18 months out.

## Updated Correlation Matrix (2026)

Sector pair Correlation regime now Driver Semis ↔ Semis Very high (0.85+) Shared hyperscaler capex Semis ↔ Industrials 0.75 and rising Data center BOM overlap Semis ↔ Utilities (regulated, nuclear-heavy) Newly correlated (0.5–0.7) PPA linkage Semis ↔ Energy (oil & gas) Still low / slightly positive Natural gas peakers a marginal driver Semis ↔ Uranium miners Newly correlated Spot uranium +25% Jan 2026, broke $100/lb

## Part III — The Future: Power as the Binding Constraint

The interesting question now is not “will chip stocks go up?” It is “what is the binding constraint, and which stocks own it?”

The answer, increasingly, is electrons.

## The 2028–2030 Power Cliff

The conditional offtake pipeline between data centers and small modular reactor (SMR) projects has grown from 25 GW at end-2024 to 45 GW today — but the first commercial SMRs (Kairos Hermes 2, X-energy XE-100, Oklo Aurora) don’t come online until 2028–2030 at the earliest, with most fleet-scale deployments slipping into the early 2030s. Microreactors might arrive in 2027–2028, but at scales (5–20 MW) that are interesting for industrial sites, not for gigawatt campuses.

That gap — between when the demand exists and when the generation arrives — is the squeeze. It explains:

- Why Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, and Google are racing to lock in existing nuclear PPAs (Three Mile Island, Susquehanna, Comanche Peak, Calvert Cliffs in negotiation) rather than waiting for new build.
- Why natural gas turbines (GE Vernova, Mitsubishi Power, Siemens Energy) have multi-year backlogs.
- Why uranium spot prices broke $100/lb in January 2026 even as U.S. domestic concentrate production fell 44% YoY in Q3 2025.
- Why FERC’s blocking of the AWS-Talen Cumulus expansion (citing grid cost allocation concerns) became market-moving news — regulatory bottlenecks are now part of the chip thesis.

## What Could Break the Correlation

A bull-case investor in the chip stack now has to track a checklist that, five years ago, would have looked irrelevant:

1. Power supply timing. If SMR deployments slip from 2030 to 2033, hyperscaler capacity additions get capped, and the chip BOM rolls over. This is the single biggest risk to the correlation trade.
2. Hyperscaler capex discipline. Four buyers, all of whom can guide capex down on a single earnings call. The 2000 analog: Intel’s September warning broke the entire chain.
3. Inference-side efficiency. If model efficiency (smaller models, distillation, on-device, ASIC purpose-built for inference) compresses tokens-per-watt by 10x, the power story softens, and the utility re-rating reverses faster than the chip re-rating.
4. Geopolitics. TSMC’s Taiwan concentration is the single point of failure for the entire stack. The Arizona ramp is real but partial.
5. Valuation gravity. Intel currently trades at 108x forward earnings — the third-highest in the Nasdaq 100. Cisco at the March 2000 peak was 472x. The math is not yet at dot-com extremes, but the dispersion within the SOX is widening, and a handful of names are doing the Cisco impression.

## The Dot-Com Comparison, Honestly

The bear case writes itself: same parabolic move, same narrative inevitability, same correlation across formerly unrelated sectors. Michael Burry has explicitly compared current semi conditions to the final months of 1999–2000.

But there are real differences worth naming. NVIDIA’s trailing P/E is roughly 30–35x against 65% revenue growth and expanding margins. Cisco at its peak had a 472x P/E against decelerating fundamentals. Hyperscaler capex is funded out of free cash flow from the four most profitable software businesses in history — not, as in 2000, out of VC equity and telecom debt. And the demand signal (training compute, inference workloads, agentic systems) has a measurable physical analog (megawatt-hours consumed) that 1999 internet eyeballs never had.

The honest read is that the trade is not a bubble in the dot-com sense, but it is concentrated, correlated, and increasingly leveraged to a single physical bottleneck. That is a different kind of risk, and it needs to be modeled differently.

## What This Means for an Investor Framework

If you are sizing the AI trade as a whole, the implication is straightforward: stop thinking about semis as a sector and start thinking about it as one leg of a three-legged stool (chips, industrials, power). Decorrelating exposure across the legs is harder than it looks because the legs are now correlated. The actual diversification has to happen outside the AI capex stack — defensives, international, value cyclicals — not by rotating from NVIDIA into Vertiv.

A few framework moves that follow from the analysis:

- Foundry over fabless if your concern is valuation. TSMC at 24x is the cheapest exposure to the entire stack and benefits regardless of which design house wins.
- Power infrastructure over generation if your concern is execution. Quanta, Eaton, GE Vernova capture the buildout whether or not any specific SMR vendor ships on time.
- Nuclear incumbents over SMR pure-plays if your concern is timing. Constellation and Vistra have power flowing today; Oklo, NuScale, and Nano Nuclear are 2030+ stories priced like 2026.
- Watch FERC and PJM more than you watch CES. The bottleneck is regulatory and physical, not technological.

## Closing

For most of the semiconductor industry’s history, chip stocks correlated with chip stocks and not much else. The end markets cycled — PCs, then mobile, then auto — but the trade stayed inside a clean perimeter.

That perimeter is gone. The buyers consolidated into four hyperscalers. The supply chain consolidated into one foundry. The constraint moved from wafer capacity to grid capacity. And so the trade now stretches from a 3nm node in Hsinchu to a refurbished reactor on the Susquehanna River, with every link in between repricing on the same news cycle.

The next chapter will be written by whichever variable breaks first — power supply, hyperscaler discipline, geopolitics, or inference efficiency. The investors who get this cycle right will not be the ones who picked the right chip company. They will be the ones who correctly modeled what isn’t a chip company but moves like one anyway.

Sources: IEA Data Centre Electricity Use Report (2026), Morgan Stanley Energy Transition Research, BloombergNEF Data Center Forecast, NVIDIA FY26 earnings, TSMC Q4 2025 earnings, AMD Q1 2026 earnings, Constellation Energy 2025 10-K, Wolfe Research, JonesTrading commentary, Renaissance Macro Research, public PPA filings and announcements.

The AI infrastructure buildout is driving hyperscalers and semiconductor developers toward gigawatt-scale loads — wattage so great their fluctuating thirst for energy could throw entire grids off balance.

Shares of a lesser-known player powering this space, Advanced Energy Industries (AEIS), have soared more than 200% in the last year for its role in helping to manage some of that juice. Based in Denver, Colo., Advanced Energy builds custom converters, measuring devices and controllers that energize semiconductor gear and other high-end products.

↑ X

What Big Tech Earnings Reveal About The AI Race

NOW PLAYING What Big Tech Earnings Reveal About The AI Race

Fresh off its first-quarter earnings and a sudden stock slide, Chief Executive Steve Kelley told Investor's Business Daily, "The second half (of the year) will be better than the first half."

Advanced Energy's first-quarter results and second-quarter guidance beat Wall Street's targets on Monday, but shares slipped after hours — then closed down 10.7% the next day.

## Behind Advanced Energy's Slide

A few finer details in the earnings report pulled focus away from Advanced Energy's upped forecast.

The company's data-center business — including power solutions that maximize uptime, boost power density and limit power loss — "is seen moderating sequentially before re-acceleration in 2H," Baird analysts wrote in a May 4 note to clients.

They added that Advanced Energy's "semi(conductor) revenues of $219M (~flat% y/y; +4% q/q) were slightly below our expectations (-$7M)." Yet the Baird analysts also expect Advanced Energy's semiconductor revenue to accelerate in the second half of the year.

This projected acceleration could come as Advanced Energy, founded in 1981, brings its fifth main factory online. Kelley, the CEO, believes initial production will kick off at the new Thailand facility in "either Q4 of this year or Q1 of next year."

"It will probably take two years to fully build that factory out, so probably (by the) end of '28 we see the full incremental capacity," he said.

Kelley reiterated Advanced Energy's expectation that the facility, focused on semiconductor gear, will unlock "at least another billion dollars a year worth of capacity."

The company is also an earnings powerhouse. Adjusted earnings per share are expected to hit $9.32 this year, up more than 45% year over year.

## Geopolitical Hazards

Kelley says the company has no plans to bring production to the U.S.

"We just couldn't compete against foreign competitors with U.S. labor costs," he told IBD.

Still, when asked what keeps him up at night, Kelley nodded to geopolitics.

"You know, I think it's probably issues out of my control — things like tariffs and export control and other things that we need to react to that can affect the business."

Baird's report expands on such potential hazards.

"Operations and supply chains based in the Asia Pacific region, including China (~13% of sales) exposes AEIS to risks regarding exchange controls, currency restrictions, changes in local economic conditions, regulations and tax policies," they wrote.

## Advanced Energy's Narrowed Focus

Along with semiconductor equipment makers and data-center operators, Advanced Energy builds for industrial medical applications. The company had fingers in other pies too, but it's pulled back on sectors such as telecom and networking applications to expand the data center business.

"The payoff, you know, for engineering effort, is much better at data centers," according to CEO Kelley.

SIGN UP NOW!

Advanced Energy is currently working with four hyperscalers, two of which represent a greater share of business than the others, per Kelley. But he declined to name them.

Baird analysts called Advanced Energy "well positioned to capitalize on megatrend growth across multiple industries," adding that the firm ranks "#1 or #2 in core markets" for power conversion. But the analysts caution that much of Advanced Energy's business is concentrated in a single market and a handful of customers.

## Half Of The Business

Semiconductor equipment represents more than half of Advanced Energy's business, Kelley told IBD — and the company's 10 largest customers represented half of its sales last year, per the Baird report.

"Inability to grow or maintain customer relationships could adversely impact operations and financial condition," the analysts said.

Advanced Energy is one piece in a global and growing semiconductor puzzle. Semiconductor makers use plasma chambers for etching and deposition, and Advanced Energy develops pulse power systems for plasma chamber developers.

To illustrate the extreme precision vital to semiconductor development, Willy Shih, a professor of management practice at Harvard Business School, suggested imagining a blown-up version of a typical, 300 mm silicon wafer used in chipmaking.

"All of these tool makers are making things with really fine critical dimensions," Shih told IBD.

For example, he said, if you scaled up a dinner plate-sized wafer so the "diameter was equivalent to the distance between the George Washington Bridge in NYC and the SF-Oakland Bay Bridge in California, then the size hole they would etch would be about the size of a thumbnail."

Shih added, "You need a lot of precision in the tools, and that means ultra-stable power with no fluctuations and noise on it."

## Semiconductor Peers

In the semiconductor industry, Advanced Energy's peers include Applied Materials (AMAT), Lam Research (LRCX), Eagle Harbor Technologies, and Trumpf. All four facilitate pulse power for chip gear, among a range of other services.

Kelley claims that around 75% of Advanced Energy's product revenue comes from sole-source products — in-house tech that makes it tricky for competitors to nip at the company's heels.

"That allows us to get a better price for our technology, and to keep our margins at levels that are attractive to investors," he said.

Advanced Energy has acquired at least 12 companies and brands to date to expand its power management offerings. Such targets include Airity Technologies, maker of high-voltage power converters, which Advanced Energy bought for an undisclosed sum in 2024.

Apparent moats aside, Advanced Energy is one player in a much larger, AI-driven semiconductor and data-center boom. A correction in demand could rattle it and other toolmakers.

In a February report on semiconductor sector growth, Deloitte cautioned that "2027 and 2028 could diverge sharply from current expectations." If AI software monetization and power availability lags, or if a major breakthrough in AI model efficiency upsets chip demand, projections that seem reasonable today could go sideways, the firm said.

## Advanced Energy Stock

But, in 2026, Advanced Energy stock remains on a solid trajectory. Shares have climbed almost 70% this year. The stock is currently standing on a floor at its 50-day moving average, MarketSurge shows.

Shares have a strong IBD Digital Composite Rating of 94. The 1-99 score measures a stock's fundamental and technical metrics, pitting them against all other stocks. So, regardless of industry group, Advanced Energy stock ranks in the leading 6% of all stocks.

The stock also has a promising Relative Strength Rating of 95, putting its 12-month performance in the top 5% of all stocks.

When Inflation Crashes the AI Party – The Cheap Investor

May 12, 2026

# When Inflation Crashes the AI Party

The April CPI report just reminded chip investors that rates still matter.

---

It turns out artificial intelligence can’t outrun a hot inflation report. This morning, the Bureau of Labor Statistics confirmed that April’s Consumer Price Index rose 3.8% year-over-year, the highest reading since May 2023, and the semiconductor sector reacted about as gracefully as someone slipping on ice. The iShares Semiconductor ETF sank 5% on the session. Qualcomm plummeted 13%, its worst day since 2020. Micron, which led the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite to record closing highs just yesterday, reversed course and fell more than 10%.

That’s not a blip. That’s the market having a moment of clarity.

Let me explain why this one stings differently.

Sponsored

$1 Billion Money Manager: “Trump’s About to RUIN Elon’s SpaceX IPO”

Donald Trump never forgets an insult. And according to this Mar-a-Lago regular, he believes Trump’s about to take his revenge on Elon Musk.

How? By releasing a radical new AI model more than 1,000X more powerful than Elon’s Grok… just in time to leapfrog Elon’s SpaceX IPO.

What’s Trump up to? And how could it send shares of one AI stock (not SpaceX) soaring?

Click here for the full story.

---

## What the numbers actually said

Headline CPI: 3.8% year-over-year. That’s up from 3.3% in March and above the Wall Street consensus of 3.7%. Month-over-month, prices rose 0.6%. Core CPI, which strips out food and energy, climbed 2.8% annually, with the monthly core reading hitting 0.4%, the highest since January 2025 and well above the 0.3% that economists had expected.

Energy is the headline driver. Energy costs jumped 17.9% annually, the steepest increase since September 2022, driven mostly by gasoline, up 28.4%, and fuel oil, up 54.3%. The figures came in above forecasts as the oil shock triggered by the war with Iran continues to push prices higher. Consumers paid a national average of $4.50 per gallon as of Tuesday, up from about $3.14 a year ago.

But here’s where it gets uncomfortable: this isn’t just an energy story. Shelter costs rose 0.6% after easing in prior months, indicating that inflation is a problem beyond the Iran war’s impacts. The tariff-sensitive apparel category increased 0.6% and airline fares accelerated 2.8%, putting the 12-month gain at 20.7%. The report also contained bad news for workers, as real average hourly wages slipped 0.5% for the month and fell 0.3% annually.

When shelter, food, and apparel are all moving in the same direction as gasoline, the Fed can’t just wait out a geopolitical event. That’s the part investors may not have fully absorbed yet.

---

## Why chip stocks took the hit

Going into today, chip stocks had been on an almost vertical run. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index surged 65% year-to-date in 2026, with a 10% weekly gain that pushed valuations to extremes rarely seen in modern markets. Micron jumped more than 37% last week on a wave of high-bandwidth memory orders for AI applications, then tacked on another 53% in April. In the past month, AMD surged more than 74%, while Qualcomm gained more than 39%.

Slight tangent, but it matters: Wall Street had been flashing signs of a stock market melt-up, a rapid and unexpected rise in stock prices, with some strategists drawing uncomfortable parallels to the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s. Michael Burry, who famously predicted the 2008 housing collapse, has taken a public position betting against the sector, with put options on the SOXX ETF expiring in January 2027. His concern isn’t that AI is fake. It’s that the velocity of the gains has disconnected from fundamentals.

Now, the mechanics. High-growth, high-multiple stocks are essentially long-duration assets. Their value is weighted heavily toward future cash flows, earnings years or decades out. When the discount rate used to value those future earnings rises, the present value of the whole enterprise mathematically shrinks. Rising Treasury yields, which move in lockstep with inflation expectations, are the mechanism. 10-year Treasury yields moving toward the 4.6% to 4.8% range exerts even more pressure on growth stocks. Semiconductor stocks focused on AI infrastructure could face the brunt of that pressure.

The damage today was not subtle. Qualcomm plummeted 13% and headed for its worst session since 2020. Intel dropped 8%, while On Semiconductor and Skyworks Solutions declined more than 6% each. The iShares Semiconductor ETF tracking the sector sank 5%. Micron, which led the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite to record highs on Monday, reversed course and fell more than 10%. The stock had soared more than 37% last week and around 53% last month amid a memory chip rally. West Texas Intermediate futures jumped 3% to trade above $101 per barrel.

The SOX remains up 4% over the past five days, 29% over the past month, and 60% since the beginning of the year — so perspective matters. One bad session doesn’t erase a year. But the broader question is whether AI demand can justify these multiples in a world where capital is no longer cheap.

In 2022, he predicted the worst market in a generation. He went 11-for-11. One trade returned 117% in under a month.

Now he’s speaking out again… and he says what’s coming makes both of those look like a warm-up.

Click here to hear his new prediction and get his #1 ticker free.

---

## What the Fed looks like right now

This is genuinely uncomfortable territory for monetary policy. The Fed held its benchmark rate steady at 3.50% to 3.75% at its April 29 meeting in an unusually divisive 8-4 vote, the closest since 1992. BofA Global Research now expects the Fed to remain on hold for the rest of this year, with two quarter-point cuts in July and September 2027.

According to CME FedWatch, markets on Tuesday morning were pricing in a nearly 98% chance that the Fed will hold rates steady at its next meeting in June and through most of 2026. But the rate hike conversation is no longer theoretical. Preston Caldwell, chief US economist at Morningstar, said the odds of a rate hike in 2026, while still less than 50%, are rising.

And there’s an added wrinkle: this new inflation alarm is what incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is walking into. Any assumption that AI could help push down inflation and allow the central bank to cut rates, a case Warsh made publicly last year, would be a tough argument to sell to the rest of the Fed committee right now.

Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist for Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, noted that the increase in core CPI suggests high energy prices are making themselves felt throughout the economy. “It doesn’t mean the Fed will pivot to rate hikes, but it does reinforce the reality that new Fed leadership won’t result in an immediate dovish shift.”

That is not an environment where growth stocks get re-rated higher.

---

## What I’m watching from here

A few things worth tracking as genuine open questions, not a checklist:

- Core PCE (late May): The Fed’s preferred inflation measure. If it confirms what CPI is showing, any remaining case for a 2026 rate cut disappears entirely.
- 10-year Treasury yield: Analysts flagged the 4.6% to 4.8% range as the zone where semiconductor valuations face real structural pressure. Watch where it settles over the next week.
- The Iran war and energy supply: Economists say the inflationary effects of the war could take weeks or months to unwind. Even if more oil tankers get through the Strait of Hormuz, it may be a while before the whole supply chain starts working again.
- Applied Materials earnings (Thursday): AMAT sells fab equipment to virtually every major chip foundry on the planet. Its results read as a leading indicator for semiconductor capital spending over the next 6 to 12 months. Worth watching closely.
- Memory chip fundamentals vs. valuations: Micron’s parabolic run was driven in part by genuine HBM memory constraints for AI workloads. That underlying demand is real. But the shortfall in some areas stems from rapid price increases in memory chips, and memory chip specialists are building capacity that should stabilize pricing and lead to much smaller revenue increases in the future. Strong fundamentals and stretched valuations are two separate conversations.

Here’s where I’m at: the AI buildout thesis hasn’t broken. Data center demand is real. Memory is genuinely constrained. The chips have already been ordered and are in backlog, data centers are under construction, and the numbers for the next 12 months are likely solid. The long-term case for owning the picks-and-shovels of this cycle is intact.

But “intact thesis” and “reasonable entry point” are two very different things. A 3.8% CPI reading in a world where everyone’s uncle is talking chip stocks is not the moment to add risk at any price. It’s the moment for patience, and for watching whether the next few inflation readings give the Fed any room to breathe at all.

The AI hype train isn’t derailed. It just hit a macro wall it hadn’t encountered in a while.

## Semiconductor concentration is making the rally potent-and fragile

This is a decision point now, not a retrospective. The S&P 500 has pushed to record highs past 7,000, while semiconductor stocks make up 18% of the S&P 500, a more-than-two-decade high. That concentration is what makes this moment so charged. If AI infrastructure demand is still climbing, this leadership can keep compounding. If it is flattening, the market is leaning too hard on one part of the economy.

Ask Aime: How will semiconductor concentration impact the S&P 500's trajectory towards 7,000?

The bull case has real fuel. In a recent selloff, the benchmark fell 1.2% while a gauge of chipmakers sank 4%, showing where the pain was concentrated. Large cloud and platform companies are also expected to spend nearly $700 billion into capital expenses this year, which supports the argument that the AI buildout is still driving demand.

Ask Aime: Is now the right time to invest in semiconductor stocks, given their high concentration in the S&P 500?

But bears have a live argument too. After the S&P 500 and Nasdaq hit new records, futures were little changed the next session. That does not look like a broad, effortless bull market. It says leadership is still thin. Even Micron MU+5.14% crossing $1 trillion in market capitalization looked more like a crown jewel moving the index than a sign that the whole market had caught up.

When one sector is doing most of the work, investors are not just betting on AI demand. They are betting that concentration can survive a shift in momentum.

## Earnings are repricing the full compute stack

The market is not just digesting one quarter. It is reassigning value across the infrastructure layer of AI, from processors to memory to networking. That is why semiconductor and IT hardware stocks rallied sharply since late March, while software companies have mostly struggled. Right now, investors are paying up for the rails first, not the apps later.

### Gartner's 2026 outlook points to breadth, not a one-chip story

The key number is not just one company's beat or miss. Gartner says the world will spend$1.3 trillion on semiconductors in 2026, the strongest growth in two decades. Just as important, that growth is not limited to one corner of the market: memory chips and networking capabilities will play a major role in the boom, alongside AI processing, data-center networking, and power.

If demand were only about inference chips, the trade would be narrower and more fragile. When memory, networking, and power all move together, the market starts valuing a broader AI-infrastructure buildout rather than a single product cycle.

### ETF flows show institutions are still adding exposure

This is where the repricing becomes harder to dismiss as short-term hype. US ETF flows hit$167.2 billion in April 2026, and large-growth and technology ETFs both set monthly inflow records. Meanwhile, technology stocks drove more than half of its performance in the S&P 500 during the month.

### Nvidia remains the clearest single-point test

Nvidia is still the centerpiece of the global AI boom, and its earnings are being read as a key test of whether AI infrastructure demand remains intact. Ahead of the report, Marvell Technology rose 7.8%, Intel gained 6.3% and Micron added 3.6%, while the Philadelphia SE Semiconductor index advanced 2.9%.

If Nvidia NVDA-1.45% and the broader group show that demand is still holding up across processors, memory, networking, and power, the rerating can widen. If not, the recent move may look too fast for the underlying adoption curve.

## What would confirm the AI infrastructure thesis-and what would break it

With chip stocks at 18% of the S&P 500, earnings are no longer just company updates. They are a stress test for whether AI demand is still moving up the curve or starting to flatten just as the market leans hardest on one leadership group.

### Confirmation would show up across the stack

The cleanest confirmation is breadth, not one headline beat. Gartner's outlook argues the 2026 semiconductor boom is being driven not only by AI processors, but also by memory chips and networking capabilities. If that breadth shows up in guidance, pricing, and product mix, investors can keep treating semis as the infrastructure layer of a larger shift.

Nvidia remains the clearest single-point stress test because it is still the centerpiece of the global AI boom. But the better read is what happens around it. If chip and IT hardware names keep their recent strength while software continues to lag, that would reinforce the idea that investors still prefer the rails over the apps. That divergence has already been visible since semiconductor and IT hardware stocks rallied sharply since late March.

A quieter but important confirmation would be power and sensing staying relevant in the trade, not just compute. Companies tied to power and sensing chips still fit the narrative if the market keeps rewarding the full infrastructure buildout.

### The invalidation signals are straightforward

The main risk is simple: if earnings fail to confirm demand across the stack, or if leadership narrows back to one or two names while the rest of the group fades, the rally becomes harder to defend as a broad infrastructure cycle.

In a concentrated tape, the practical stance is not to fight the curve blindly, but to size for the verdict. If the next reports confirm demand across processors, memory, networking, and power, the rerating can widen beyond the obvious leaders. If not, this stops looking like an adoption story and starts looking more like a momentum unwind in a crowded leadership group.

The backdrop has not been clean. The Dow crossed 50,600 as traders navigated geopolitical pressure and a tug of war over AI chips. Semiconductors kept moving anyway. The SOX posted nearly 80% gains so far in 2026, which says investors still see the sector as the infrastructure layer of the AI buildout rather than a passing headline trade.

### Nvidia earnings became the sector's stress test

Earlier this month, chip stocks rebounded into Nvidia NVDA-- earnings as investors looked for proof AI infrastructure demand remains strong. That remains the key test. If spending, margins, and guidance hold, the sector can keep its premium. If not, concentration stops being a support and becomes the problem.

## The upside is broadening beyond the obvious GPU names

The next question is not whether AI demand exists. It is whether the upside is still confined to a few accelerator names or spreading through the rest of the semiconductor stack.

### Sector strength is showing up across more of the chain

SMH is up over 20% year to date while the broader market is only slightly green. That strength is not limited to the most obvious AI winners; it is also visible in equipment, analog, power, and packaging names that sit lower in the value chain. A narrow rally can break on sentiment alone. A broader one is a stronger sign that adoption is moving through more of the infrastructure layer.

The available evidence does support the idea that the turn is widening. Reports on the sector's strength point beyond the headline AI trade to analog and power makers tied to factory automation, data centers, and grid infrastructure. That does not prove every adjacent name is equally positioned, but it does suggest the upcycle is not limited to GPUs alone.

### AI economics are concentrated, but the buildout touches more than one niche

There is also a structural reason this broadening matters. AI chips now drive roughly half of total revenue even though they represent less than 0.2% of total unit volume. In other words, a small slice of chip volume is capturing a large share of industry economics. That makes the supporting layers-fabrication, packaging, power delivery, and testing-important to watch.

That helps explain the attention on wafer fabrication equipment, analog and power management, foundry capacity, and packaging. TSMC TSM-- has benefited from renewed investor interest in AI-related stocks, while SMH's breadth shows capital is still rotating through multiple parts of the semiconductor chain, not just the most visible accelerator names.

### What to watch from here

- Does leadership stay broad across SMH, or does it narrow back to a handful of names?
- Does demand in test, analog, power, and equipment remain firm as a sign that capex is broad-based?
- Does foundry and packaging capacity stay tight enough to support the rest of the stack?

It is whether the S-curve is still steepening in a way that shows up in earnings quality, not just headline demand. That is why the recent Micron move matters. After UBS pointed to long-term supply agreements that could structurally transform the company's earnings profile, the stock rose because investors saw a clearer path to more durable earnings power.

### The bear case only needs flattening economics

Bears do not need a collapse in AI spending. They only need the economics to flatten. The sector's central tension is that AI chips now drive roughly half of total revenue while representing less than 0.2% of total unit volume. That is powerful while demand stays tight and pricing holds. It leaves less room for guidance misses, margin pressure, or weaker supply plans.

### The market has already shown it wants fundamentals

Investors rotated out of some AI names earlier this year because of sentiment rather than fundamentals, then rotated back as sector breadth improved and SMH climbed over 20% year to date. That suggests the rally still needs confirmation, not just a compelling story.

Positioning lens: treat earnings as a filter, not a verdict. If results show the economics are hardening across more than the top accelerator names, the next leg can come from the rest of the stack. If not, the market is more likely to punish concentration.

# AI and Semiconductor Momentum Continue Driving U.S. Equity Rally

May 12, 2026

●

By: Peter Valderama

Share this post on X Share this post on LinkedIn Share this post on Facebook

Wall Street’s rally is increasingly becoming a story of two markets.

On one side are the companies directly tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing, and hyperscale computing demand — stocks that continue pushing major indexes toward fresh highs. On the other side sits a broader market still wrestling with elevated interest rates, geopolitical uncertainty, slowing consumer trends, and questions about how sustainable the AI-driven surge really is.

That divide is becoming one of the most important themes for investors in 2026.

Over the past several months, U.S. equity markets have remained heavily concentrated around technology megacaps, semiconductor manufacturers, AI infrastructure firms, and companies tied to domestic chip production. According to discussions highlighted by Reuters, Wall Street analysts, and investor forums, optimism surrounding artificial intelligence demand continues fueling capital flows into semiconductor-related equities despite growing macroeconomic concerns.

The result is a market rally powered largely by a relatively small group of AI-linked companies.

For investors, the critical question now is whether the next phase of the bull market broadens into sectors like industrials, financials, healthcare, and cyclicals — or whether the rally remains dependent on a narrow concentration of technology giants.

That answer could shape portfolio performance for the rest of the year.

## The AI Trade Continues to Dominate Wall Street

The AI investment theme has evolved from a speculative technology trend into the central force driving U.S. equity market performance.

Since the explosive rise of generative AI following the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022, investors have aggressively rotated toward companies benefiting from AI infrastructure demand. Semiconductor firms, cloud providers, networking companies, and data center operators have emerged as some of the market’s biggest winners.

The logic behind the trade is straightforward.

Artificial intelligence requires enormous computational power. That means rising demand for advanced GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, networking systems, cooling technologies, cloud infrastructure, and electricity generation.

As enterprises rush to deploy AI capabilities across industries, investors increasingly view semiconductor manufacturers and infrastructure providers as foundational beneficiaries of a multi-year technology cycle.

According to estimates from McKinsey & Company, generative AI could add between $2.6 trillion and $4.4 trillion annually to the global economy. Meanwhile, IDC projects global AI infrastructure spending will continue rising sharply through the decade as corporations expand AI-related capital expenditures.

That narrative has fueled extraordinary investor enthusiasm surrounding semiconductor stocks.

Companies involved in chip manufacturing, AI accelerators, advanced packaging, and cloud infrastructure have become dominant contributors to broader index performance. Technology megacaps now represent an unusually large share of total S&P 500 gains, reinforcing concerns about market concentration.

## Semiconductor Optimism Is Extending Beyond AI

The semiconductor rally is no longer driven solely by AI software excitement.

Another major factor supporting investor sentiment is the growing push toward domestic chip manufacturing and supply-chain resilience.

Governments across the United States, Europe, and Asia are increasingly treating semiconductors as strategic national infrastructure. The COVID-era chip shortages, combined with geopolitical tensions surrounding Taiwan and China, fundamentally changed how policymakers and investors view semiconductor supply chains.

The U.S. CHIPS and Science Act accelerated this trend by encouraging domestic semiconductor investment and manufacturing expansion. Since then, major technology firms and chipmakers have announced tens of billions of dollars in new manufacturing facilities and infrastructure projects.

Recent reports surrounding potential manufacturing partnerships between large technology companies and U.S.-based chip producers have further strengthened optimism across the semiconductor sector.

Investors increasingly believe domestic manufacturing could become a long-term structural growth driver for semiconductor equipment suppliers, foundries, industrial automation companies, and energy infrastructure firms.

This shift is creating a broader ecosystem effect.

The AI boom is no longer benefiting only software developers. It is increasingly supporting industrials, construction firms, utilities, semiconductor equipment manufacturers, and advanced materials suppliers tied to the expanding infrastructure footprint of artificial intelligence.

## Why Market Concentration Is Becoming a Risk

Despite strong market performance, investors are beginning to focus on a growing concern: concentration risk.

A relatively small number of companies are currently driving a disproportionately large share of index gains.

Historically, narrow rallies can become vulnerable if earnings growth fails to broaden across sectors. If investor sentiment weakens toward AI infrastructure or semiconductor spending, broader markets could face increased volatility due to the heavy weighting of technology giants within major indexes.

Analysts from Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, and other Wall Street firms have repeatedly noted that earnings growth remains unusually concentrated among large-cap technology and semiconductor companies.

That concentration creates both opportunity and risk.

On one hand, dominant AI infrastructure leaders continue generating strong revenue growth fueled by enterprise demand, cloud expansion, and capital investment cycles. On the other hand, elevated valuations leave little room for execution mistakes or slower-than-expected monetization.

Investors are increasingly debating whether the AI trade is entering a sustainable productivity cycle similar to the internet boom — or whether portions of the market are becoming overheated.

The answer may ultimately depend on whether economic growth broadens beyond technology.

## Interest Rates and Geopolitics Still Matter

One reason investors remain cautious despite strong equity performance is that the macroeconomic backdrop remains highly uncertain.

Interest rates continue to play a major role in market positioning. Although inflation pressures have moderated compared to previous years, Federal Reserve policy remains a key driver of investor sentiment.

Higher rates can pressure high-growth technology valuations by increasing discount rates and raising financing costs for capital-intensive AI infrastructure projects.

At the same time, geopolitical risks remain elevated.

Ongoing tensions involving China, Taiwan, trade policy, and strategic technology competition continue influencing semiconductor supply chains and investor expectations. Any disruption tied to advanced chip manufacturing or global trade flows could create significant volatility across technology markets.

Energy infrastructure is also emerging as a key issue.

AI data centers require enormous electricity consumption, leading investors to increasingly monitor utility providers, nuclear energy projects, grid modernization efforts, and energy infrastructure companies supporting AI expansion.

This dynamic is creating new intersections between technology investing, industrial policy, and commodity markets.

## The Rally May Need Broader Participation

A growing debate across Wall Street is whether the market can sustain momentum without broader sector participation.

Historically, durable bull markets tend to involve stronger performance from industrials, financials, transportation, consumer discretionary, and cyclical sectors alongside technology leadership.

So far, much of the market’s momentum remains concentrated within AI-linked equities.

If earnings growth begins spreading across additional sectors, the rally could become more sustainable and less vulnerable to sector-specific corrections. Stronger manufacturing activity, infrastructure investment, improving consumer demand, and stabilization in financial conditions could all contribute to broader participation.

Some investors are already positioning for this possibility by rotating selectively into industrial automation, energy infrastructure, cybersecurity, utilities, and advanced manufacturing plays linked indirectly to AI expansion.

That strategy reflects a growing realization that the AI boom may create secondary and tertiary beneficiaries across the broader economy.

## Future Trends Investors Should Watch

Several key themes are likely to shape markets over the coming quarters.

First, semiconductor demand remains one of the most important variables in the global equity rally. Investors will closely monitor chip orders, AI capital expenditures, and hyperscaler spending trends.

Second, earnings breadth will become increasingly important. Markets may become more stable if revenue growth expands beyond large-cap technology firms into industrials and cyclicals.

Third, infrastructure investing could emerge as a major long-term beneficiary of AI expansion. Utilities, energy systems, networking equipment, construction, and semiconductor manufacturing all stand to benefit from rising AI-related demand.

Finally, valuation discipline will matter more as the rally matures. Investors are increasingly differentiating between companies with sustainable AI-driven cash flow growth and those benefiting primarily from speculative momentum.

## Key Investment Insight

The current U.S. equity rally remains heavily driven by artificial intelligence infrastructure, semiconductor manufacturing, and technology megacaps — but the next phase of the market may depend on whether growth broadens across the economy.

For investors, the strongest opportunities may increasingly lie not only in headline AI leaders, but also in the broader ecosystem supporting the expansion of advanced computing infrastructure. Semiconductor manufacturing, energy systems, industrial automation, utilities, networking equipment, and domestic supply-chain development could all remain critical long-term themes.

At the same time, concentration risk is rising. Investors should closely monitor whether earnings growth spreads into financials, industrials, healthcare, and cyclical sectors or remains dependent on a narrow group of AI-linked stocks.

The AI boom continues to reshape markets, but the sustainability of this rally may ultimately depend on how broadly those economic benefits begin to spread.

# AI Energy Nexus Mining Stocks: What they are, why they matter, 2026 outlook | Skillings

Author: Charles Pitts
Published: 2026-05-31T00:30:07+00:00
Source: skillings.net (skillings.net)
Language: en

## Story

AI Energy Nexus Mining Stocks: What they are, why they matter, 2026 outlook | Skillings

SHARE

By Penny Langford

Contents

- The Energy Intensity of Artificial Intelligence
- Uranium: The Baseload Foundation
- Copper: The Electrical Conduit
- Silver: The Connectivity Enabler
- Commodity Price Forecasts for 2026
- Strategic Considerations for 2026

The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and global energy infrastructure has created a structural shift in commodity markets known as the "AI Energy Nexus." As hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google accelerate the deployment of large language models (LLMs), the demand for carbon-free baseload power and grid-level electrical infrastructure has surged. This transition is transforming the fundamental outlook for specific mining sectors: primarily uranium, copper, and silver: that are essential to building and powering the next generation of data centers.

By 2026, global data center infrastructure spending is projected to reach approximately US$7 trillion, with roughly US$1.3 trillion directed specifically toward power generation and transmission. For operators and investors, understanding the specific mining equities positioned at the center of this nexus is critical for navigating the 2026 market landscape.

## The Energy Intensity of Artificial Intelligence

The power requirements for training and running LLMs are orders of magnitude higher than traditional cloud computing. Training a single frontier model can consume tens of gigawatt-hours (GWh) of electricity. However, the true long-term load comes from inference: the ongoing process of serving user queries: which drives a sustained, massive demand for 24/7 baseload power.

This surge is occurring as the U.S. and global power grids face a simultaneous push for decarbonization and industrial reshoring. The result is a tightening power market where tech giants are no longer just customers of utilities; they are becoming direct partners in nuclear and renewable projects.

## Uranium: The Baseload Foundation

Uranium is the primary beneficiary of the AI Energy Nexus due to nuclear power’s ability to provide high-capacity, carbon-free baseload electricity. Tech companies have increasingly sought behind-the-meter power agreements with nuclear operators to secure reliable energy for their AI clusters.

### Cameco (TSX: CCO | NYSE: CCJ)

As the world’s second-largest uranium miner, Cameco represents the most established play in the nuclear fuel cycle. The company controls roughly 15% of global production and provides critical refining and conversion services. Into 2026, Cameco is positioned to benefit from a rising realized price environment as long-term contracts are repriced at higher levels. With adjusted earnings projected to grow significantly through 2025 and 2026, Cameco remains a core holding for those tracking the uranium super-cycle.

### NexGen Energy (TSX: NXE | NYSE: NXE)

While Cameco provides production stability, NexGen Energy offers leverage as a developer. The company is advancing the Rook I project in the Athabasca Basin, which is slated to be one of the largest and highest-grade uranium mines in the world. As the market looks toward the structural deficits of the late 2020s, NexGen’s ability to bring large-scale supply online will be essential to meeting the demand from new Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) and traditional reactor life extensions.

## Copper: The Electrical Conduit

If uranium is the fuel of the AI boom, copper is the physical medium that delivers that energy. Data centers require extensive copper cabling, while the broader grid requires substantial upgrades in transformers and transmission lines to handle the increased load.

### BHP (ASX: BHP | NYSE: BHP)

BHP is a global leader in copper production, particularly through its Escondida and Spence operations in Chile. The company’s scale and low-cost structure make it a primary beneficiary of the forecast US$11,400/t copper price in 2026. As a diversified major, BHP provides exposure to the AI nexus while mitigating the idiosyncratic risks associated with single-asset juniors. The company's focus on high-quality copper assets aligns with the "grid metal" demand driven by AI-related infrastructure.

### Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX)

Freeport-McMoRan is a copper pure-play with massive operations in North and South America, as well as Indonesia. Given that AI data centers and electrification are driving a 25% increase in projected U.S. electricity demand by 2030, Freeport’s significant domestic production footprint in the United States offers a strategic advantage. The company's technological initiatives in copper leaching could also provide a margin-enhancing boost to production as demand peaks in 2026.

## Silver: The Connectivity Enabler

Silver's role in the AI Energy Nexus is often overlooked but remains vital. It is the most conductive metal on Earth, making it essential for the high-end electronics, semiconductors, and electrical contacts used in data center hardware and renewable energy systems.

### Coeur Mining (NYSE: CDE)

Coeur Mining has significantly expanded its silver production capacity through the expansion of the Rochester mine in Nevada. As industrial demand from the electronics and solar sectors continues to grow, Coeur is well-positioned to capture the upside. While silver is often subject to macro-driven volatility, its fundamental role in the "connectivity" aspect of AI infrastructure provides a solid demand floor.

## Commodity Price Forecasts for 2026

The following table summarizes the 2026 base-case forecasts for the primary commodities driving the AI Energy Nexus, based on current institutional research and market trends.

| Commodity | 2026 Base-Case Forecast | Primary AI Driver |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uranium | US$95.00 – US$105.00 /lb | Nuclear baseload for data centers |
| Copper | US$11,400 /t (LME) | Grid transmission and data center cabling |
| Silver | US$28.00 – US$32.00 /oz | Electronics and high-end connectivity |

Note: Forecasts are subject to change based on global macro conditions and the pace of AI infrastructure deployment.

## Strategic Considerations for 2026

The transition toward an AI-driven energy landscape is not without risks. Investors and operators must monitor several key variables:

1. Regulatory Hurdles: The build-out of nuclear power and transmission lines often faces long permitting timelines. Any acceleration or delay in these processes will directly impact the demand timelines for uranium and copper.
2. Technological Efficiency: Improvements in AI algorithm efficiency or hardware power consumption could shift the demand curve. However, history suggests that increased efficiency often leads to higher overall usage (Jevons Paradox).
3. M&A Activity: The 2026 mining M&A landscape is expected to be dominated by majors acquiring high-quality assets to secure supply for the transition. Companies like BHP and Cameco are likely to remain active in this space.

The AI Energy Nexus represents more than a cyclical trend; it is a structural realignment of how the world produces and consumes energy. By focusing on the miners that provide the fuel and the conduits for this power, market participants can better position themselves for the hardware-intensive reality of the 2026 AI boom.

# A cyclical boom is eating the whole index: memory, semis, and the active manager's nightmare

May 27, 2026

70

2

5

Share

Markets are cyclical; there's nothing new about that. There's always some corner of the market riding a bull wave or a strong pricing environment. There was peak oil in ~2006, or the commodity bull market in ~2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. There was a wild memory cycle in ~2012 when one of the memory plants got flooded, and there have been too many crypto booms and busts to count over the past ten years.

For anyone who benchmarks to an index, I'm not sure we've ever seen anything quite like the current memory / semi cycle: a single cyclical boom that is big enough to move the whole market by itself.

In the short term, the supply of memory and semiconductors are somewhat fixed; it doesn’t really matter how strong the demand is, it takes years to build up new plants to make more of these. The AI boom has driven seemingly unlimited demand for memory and semiconductors. Combine skyrocketing demand with no immediate supply response, and memory and semiconductor prices are soaring… and taking their underlying stocks with them.

Yet Another Value Blog is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

Subscribe

Nothing in that sentence is new when it comes to cyclical booms/busts. Most big commodity industries have relatively fixed supply in the short term, and they all run through booms and busts….. but the AI boom is somewhat unique in its structure. Consider a few factors:

Scale of demand increase: most commodities tend to have pretty stable demand because they’re reasonably mature industries. A really strong economy is going to send the demand for energy up by a few percent at most. The auto cycle tends to swing on 5-10% moves in annualized new car sales. In contrast, memory demand has gone up by ~400% inside of a year or two.

Lack of supply response: Send prices up enough, and you’ll find some form of switching. When oil spikes, governments will release their strategic reserves to smooth out prices. If nat gas spikes, you’ll see switching from nat gas to coal. And it only takes a few weeks to bring on some marginal supply of nat gas / oil…. but there’s no strategic memory reserve to release from, and there’s really no alternative to memory a la nat gas / coal.

Lack of demand destruction: When oil prices double, people respond on the margin with less oil consumption. Flights get cancelled, road trips get shortened, etc. When electricity prices go up, you’ll see factories ration production. But the AI boom has shown no sign of abating, and the only demand destruction we’ve seen has come from the AI labs throttling their users to meet booming demand.

So those factors make this cycle even hotter / faster than a normal commodity cycle. Consider this: Micron did ~$1b in free cash flow in FY25 and was trading for just over $100B EV. Today, Micron is forecasted to do $100B in free cash flow in 2027. That’s right: Micron’s free cash flow is up almost 100x in ~2 years, and they’ll print almost their entire EV heading into the cycle. Again, we’ve seen cyclical booms before, but the scale and speed of this one is mind blowing!

Perhaps my memory (pun intended) is lacking, but I’m not sure we’ve ever seen a cyclical upswing like this drive an entire market before. As I write this, the S&P 500 is up ~10% YTD. Basically half of that return is coming from just four stocks: Google (~7% of the index, up 25% YTD), NVDA (~7.6% of the index, up 16% YTD), Micron (~1.6% weighting, up ~250% YTD), and AMD (~1.2% of the index; up 140% YTD).

If you broaden it out a little bit to include just AAPL, INTC, AVGO, and AMZN, 8 stocks have driven 75% of the S&P’s YTD return.

And the top 20 contributors to the S&P have generated more than all of the index’s returns YTD:

Those are large companies making massive moves! Again, it’s nothing crazy to see companies generating massive returns during a cyclical bull. What is crazy is to see it happen to companies this large and have them single handedly drive an index.

Now consider what those massive, concentrated moves mean for an active investor benchmarked to the index: if you were underweight a single one of those stocks, you’re trailing the index by a mile. If you were underweight a handful of them and long a single SaaS stock (shudders), you’re currently writing your first draft of your H1 letter explaining to your LPs why you’re trailing the index by 1500 bps.

I was in grammar school during the dotcom bubble, so I can’t claim to have personally known what it was like investing then. But you’ll read about value investors then tearing their hair out as dotcom stocks doubled seemingly every week with no fundamental value while their value stocks languished.

The current market is nowhere close to that bad. The AI beneficiaries are minting money while they’re riding the current wave. Again, Micron might do $100B in free cash flow in fiscal 2027; that’s roughly what its EV was in mid-2025!!!!

But a lot of value stocks are languishing. And while AI bulls would tell you that cycles are over, I’m somewhat skeptical that this time is different when it comes to the boom/bust nature of semis or memory. These companies are simply printing too much money for there not to be a supply response, and history suggests that a super cycle this profitable will eventually be met with a supply overbuild for the ages.

If and when that happens, it’ll be interesting to see what happens to the indices!

PS- there’s a wave of big IPOs coming (SpaceX, Anthropic, etc). These are some of the biggest companies the markets have ever seen, and they’ll almost certainly quickly get added to the indices. While they will carry a lot of AI related “factor beta”, I would guess they’ll also be less cyclical than something like Micron or AMD. So, humorously, you could live in a world where MU and AMD drive the indices up, then see their weights diluted when a new wave of mega IPOs get added to the indices, and then don’t have anywhere close to as big of an impact if their stocks go down as the cycle ends. Being an active manager is hard!

# The AI Trade Just Had Its Worst Stretch in Months. Here Are 3 Reasons the Sell-Off Could Be a Buying Opportunity. | The Motley Fool

Author: Daniel Sparks
Published: 2026-06-10T02:03:00+00:00
Source: fool.com (fool.com)
Language: en

## Story

The AI Trade Just Had Its Worst Stretch in Months. Here Are 3 Reasons the Sell-Off Could Be a Buying Opportunity. | The Motley Fool

Accessibility Menu

▲ S&P 500 +---%|▲ Stock Advisor +---%Join The Motley Fool

The artificial intelligence (AI) trade just went through its roughest stretch in months. After a nine-week run higher, the major indexes pulled back last week, and the selling peaked on Friday, when the Nasdaq Composite fell about 4.2% -- its steepest single-day drop since early 2025. Chip stocks took the worst of it, with the broad semiconductor group sliding about 10% in that single session.

The sell-off appeared to be tied to several things. Broadcom (AVGO 1.12%) posted record results but stopped short of raising its full-year outlook for AI chips, a hotter-than-expected May jobs report pushed bond yields higher and revived worries about a possible interest rate increase, and renewed tensions in the Middle East added to the unease. All told, about $1.3 trillion in value came off U.S.-traded chipmakers on Friday.

But the businesses behind those stocks look as healthy as ever. And shares briefly bounced, with the Nasdaq rising about 0.9% on Monday as the names that led the drop led the recovery. But skittishness in the sector returned on Tuesday.

Here are three reasons last week's decline could prove to be an opportunity rather than a warning.

Image source: Getty Images.

## 1. The spending behind the trade hasn't slowed

First of all, it's worth noting that massive AI spending seems to just be getting started. The four biggest U.S. cloud operators collectively plan to spend around $700 billion on capital expenditures to support data centers and the chips that fill them in 2026 -- nearly double what they spent in 2025. And three of the four actually raised those plans when they reported in late April.

Much of that money, of course, flows directly to the chip designers that sold off last week, and a good chunk of it is already committed. On its fiscal second-quarter earnings call (covering the period ended May 3, 2026), Broadcom's management reiterated that it expects its AI chip revenue to be above $100 billion in fiscal 2027, pointing to contracted demand from a small group of large customers that includes Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

A few rough sessions for the stock -- and the broader chip sector -- don't change those order books.

## 2. The businesses are still growing fast

Last week's selling had little to do with how these companies are performing. Nvidia (NVDA 0.43%) reported results for its fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the period ended April 26, 2026) last month that were the best in its history. Revenue rose 85% year over year to a record $81.6 billion, its data center business grew 92%, and management guided for about $91 billion in the current quarter. The company also lifted its dividend and added $80 billion to its share repurchase program.

"The buildout of AI factories -- the largest infrastructure expansion in human history -- is accelerating at extraordinary speed," said Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang in the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings release.

Broadcom told investors a similar story. In early June, the chipmaker posted record fiscal second-quarter revenue of $22.2 billion, up 48% year over year, with its AI chip revenue alone jumping 143% to $10.8 billion. It also guided for AI chip sales to grow more than 200% in the current quarter.

## 3. Valuations have come back to earth

The pullback did something useful, too. It let some air out of valuations that had climbed in a hurry. Semiconductor stocks had run up sharply through the spring, and Nvidia alone shed close to $280 billion in market value during the slide.

After that reset, the numbers look more reasonable than they have in some time. As of this writing, Nvidia trades around $208, down about 12% from its mid-May high, and changes hands at about 32 times earnings.

For a business still expanding revenue at better than 80% a year, a valuation multiple like this hardly seems stretched.

# The Nasdaq is Rebounding on Monday. But Rising Oil Prices Still Threaten the AI Trade.

By Thomas Richmond Published Jun 8, 11:21AM EDT

### Quick Read

QQQ bounced 2% Monday after its worst week in over a year, still holding a 15% year-to-date gain.

SPY fell 2.5% Friday as a blowout jobs report pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.47%, compressing valuations on AI-heavy tech stocks.

Iran-Israel strikes sent WTI crude near $96 a barrel, threatening to reignite inflation and keep yields elevated against the chip-led rebound.

Don't wait: the analyst who called NVIDIA in 2010 just revealed his top 10 AI stocks. See the full list FREE now.

### How to Add Us to Google News

Sending You to Google News in 3

Wall Street opened Monday with mixed performance. Chip stocks are rebounding, lifting NASDAQ futures and pulling the index back from Friday’s brutal session. However, the Dow is heading in the opposite direction as crude oil prices jump amid fresh Middle East tensions. CNBC’s Morgan Brennan summed up the setup on air Monday morning, noting the NASDAQ was down more than 4% on Friday, June 5, its worst day in more than a year.

Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) closed Friday with a one-week decline of 4.5%, and is indicated higher in early Monday trading, with the most recent print showing a 1.84% bounce. The year-to-date gain still stands at 14.77%, a reminder that the AI-led rally has plenty of cushion even after the worst single session in over a year.

## Chip Stocks Fight Back After Friday’s Bloodbath

Semiconductors, the leading group of the AI trade, are the engine of Monday’s recovery. After Friday’s slide that saw the NASDAQ fall more than 4%, the S&P 500 drop more than 2.5%, and the Dow fall nearly 700 points, buyers are stepping back into the names that took the most damage. The bounce looks like a textbook relief move in the market’s most crowded trade.

## Strong Jobs Report Becomes Bad News for Stocks

Brennan attributed the slide to macro forces, saying “the slide coming on the back of the strong monthly jobs report, which boosted yields on treasury bonds and sparked worries higher borrowing costs could hit tech companies investing heavily on artificial intelligence.” The Bureau of Labor Statistics’ May report showed nonfarm payrolls at 159,001 thousand, the highest level in the series and a clear signal of labor market durability.

That strength pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 4.47% as of June 4, sitting in the 93.5 percentile of its past-year range, according to FRED data. Higher long rates compress the present value of future earnings, and they raise the cost of the enormous capital expenditure programs funding data centers and AI infrastructure. That mechanism is the rate-driven risk hanging over every AI-heavy tech name.

## Oil Prices Become the Market’s New Problem

Oil prices jumped after Iran and Israel exchanged strikes, raising fears about escalation in the Middle East. WTI crude was already elevated, closing at $95.96 per barrel on June 1 and sitting in the 82.8 percentile of its past-year range.

For the AI trade, the oil move matters beyond the obvious hit to Dow components in transports and industrials. Higher crude feeds headline inflation, with CPI already running at 332.4 in April, up 0.6% month over month. Hotter inflation numbers keep upward pressure on yields, which is the same dynamic that pushed tech valuations lower on Friday.

## The Tug-of-War for Investors

The market is now caught between a chip-led rebound and two pressures pushing in the same direction. Yields are firm because of the jobs report. Oil is firm because of geopolitics. Both feed the same inflation channel, and both raise the discount rate applied to AI capex and growth multiples. The VIX reflects the strain, jumping to 21.51 on June 5, a 39.7% daily spike that pulled the fear gauge into elevated territory.

Monday’s rebound shows investors still want exposure to chip and AI stocks, but the recovery remains fragile. Higher oil prices and elevated Treasury yields could continue to pressure the sector by keeping inflation and borrowing costs high. Investors should keep a close eye on crude oil and the 10-year Treasury yield to see whether the rebound continues or loses momentum.
